articles.title: Four decades, thousands of test hours and one big milestone: India’s Kaveri engine story
articles.summary: India's homegrown Kaveri dry engine has come through a round of high-altitude and flight trials in Russia, posting a peak dry thrust of 48.5 kilonewtons,
articles.body: India's homegrown Kaveri dry engine has come through a round of high-altitude and flight trials in Russia, posting a peak dry thrust of 48.5 kilonewtons, well above the roughly 46 kN it was meant to deliver. The engine, built by the Defence Research and Development Organisation's Gas Turbine Research Establishment, is meant to power Ghatak, India's planned stealth unmanned combat aerial vehicle.The Kaveri Derivative Engine is a non-afterburning version of the original Kaveri, built for aircraft that do not need the additional thrust an afterburner provides. Dry thrust simply refers to thrust generated without one. The trials ran at two Russian institutions, the Central Institute of Aviation Motors and the Gromov Flight Research Institute. At the former, the engine was subjected to conditions mimicking high-altitude flight, where air pressure and temperature both drop sharply. Engineers then moved to flight tests using a modified Ilyushin Il-76 flying testbed, with one of its standard engines swapped out for the Kaveri, allowing the new engine to be evaluated in actual flight without being integrated into its final intended aircraft. The team tested it across varying ambient pressures, Mach numbers and thrust demands, partly on the ground and partly in the air.A reading of 48.5 kN against a target of 46 kN suggests the engine now has some margin to spare. The Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification will examine the test data before granting airworthiness clearance, though certification and integration with the platform still remain before any operational use can be considered.The story of how India got here goes back to 1986, when the Kaveri programme was launched to develop an indigenous powerplant for the Light Combat Aircraft Tejas. Formally sanctioned in 1989 with a completion target of 1996, the project involved building a low-bypass turbofan with an afterburner, along with its compressor, combustion chamber, turbine and control systems.The Kaveri ran into serious developmental trouble almost immediately, struggling with high-temperature materials, turbine blades capable of withstanding extreme internal conditions, compressor development and achieving the required thrust-to-weight ratio. The original Kaveri was designed to produce about 81 kN of thrust but managed only around 70 kN in its earlier configuration, while also exceeding its intended weight target of 1,100 kg. That shortfall, combined with limited domestic testing infrastructure and restricted access to advanced foreign technology, meant the engine could never meet Tejas's requirements, forcing the fighter to adopt foreign powerplants instead.Rather than shelving the programme, DRDO redirected it, pursuing a dry, non-afterburning derivative suited to different propulsion needs, eventually finding a new purpose in the Ghatak UCAV. Along the way, the programme built up substantial indigenous expertise, multiple prototypes, more than 3,200 hours of testing, a qualified Full Authority Digital Engine Control system, and certified high-temperature materials for aero-engine use, all validated through Il-76 flight testing that gave Indian engineers rare hands-on experience operating an indigenous gas-turbine engine in real flight conditions.That expertise is really the point of the exercise. Fighter-engine development demands far more than raw thrust, it requires mastery of compressors, turbines, combustion systems, materials science, engine controls and manufacturing, all of which the Kaveri programme forced India to build from scratch. What started as an attempt to power the country's first indigenous fighter has since evolved into a longer-term foundation for future Indian aircraft engines. The latest 48.5 kN result, then, matters less as an isolated technical milestone and more as evidence that decades of setbacks have left India with a genuine engine-development base, one that now has to be converted into a certified, production-ready powerplant for an aircraft actually waiting to fly.

articles.title: Antilia bomb scare case: HC bench recuses in NIA's appeal against bail granted to Sachin Waze
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Following two recusals, a third division bench of Bombay HC comprising Justices Girish Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale on Wednesday stayed the bail
articles.body: MUMBAI: Following two recusals, a third division bench of Bombay HC comprising Justices Girish Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale on Wednesday stayed the bail granted by a special NIA court to former police officer Sachin Waze in the five year old Antilia bomb scare and Mansukh Hiran murder case under the anti-terror law—UAPA.The Justice Kulkarni-led bench issued notice to Waze and posted the matter for hearing on October 7.When the matter originally came up on Wednesday as scheduled and listed before a division bench of Justices Bharti Dangre and Ashish Chavan, Justice Dangre asked if Waze was released or not as yet. Additional Solicitor General Anil Singh for NIA said Waze was not released. Justices Bharati Dangre and Ashish Chavan recused themselves from hearing an appeal filed by National Investigation Agency (NIA) to the bail that special trial court granted on Tuesday to dismissed police officer Sachin Waze in the five year old Antilia bomb scare and Mansukh Hiran murder case under the anti-terror law—UAPA.Waze has spent 1,999 days in custody.Justice Dangre then said she had earlier passed a reasoned order in a matter where “this very person’ (Waze) was a co-accused along with a former minister. The ASG said this was not a connected matter. Justice Dangre said she had earlier already --in September 2024--recused and directed that Waze’s matter in the NIA case not be placed before a bench where she is a party. Her 2024 order was in a plea filed by Waze to quash the proceedings against him.Justice Dangre said to the ASG, “We understand and appreciate your inconvenience’’ and expressed regret that the matter would now have to be placed before another bench.Justice Chavan—who was appointed as Judge last year--too recused saying he had as a lawyer appeared for the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in a distinctly connected matter.On Tuesday, HC division bench of Justices Sarang Kotwal and RR Bhonsale had recused itself when the ASG had mentioned the challenge and sought urgent hearing.After Justice Dangre and Justice Chavan recused in the morning, the ASG Singh representing NIA, mentioned the matter before the HC Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi to have it assigned before another bench. He said the reason he sought the CJ's intervention was since three other division benches had a Judge who had been appearing for the Central government and were representing its agencies in the case when they were lawyers. The CJ assigned the mater to Justice Kulkarni's bench, before who the NIA then went and sought a stay on Waze's release from Thane Central prison.On Feb 25, 2021, an explosives-laden SUV was found near Antilia in south Mumbai. The NIA alleged that Waze orchestrated the plot to extort wealthy individuals and project himself as a “super cop” after returning to the police force from a long suspension. According to the agency, Waze used a Scorpio owned by Mansukh Hiran, fabricated theft proceedings, and planted gelatin sticks and a threat note in the vehicle. Hiran was allegedly murdered on March 4, 2021, because he knew of the conspiracy and could expose it. Waze was arrested later that month.On Tuesday, special NIA court judge Chakor S Baviskar granting bail to Waze had held that there was “absolutely nothing on record” to infer that industrialist Mukesh Ambani or his family were ever terrorized.The NIA had alleged that Waze intended to create fear in the Ambani family, possibly to extort money. The court called this “quite hypothetical”, saying there was “literally no iota of material” to show any demand for money by Waze from the Ambanis.The judge observed that the SUV containing gelatin sticks was parked near Shikharkunj building on Carmichael Road, and not directly opposite Antilia on Altamount Road. It said the distance between the two spots was considerable, with several buildings in between. “Hence, even the threat to the alleged target does not carry that much weight so as to create terror in their or anyone’s mind,” the judge said.The court observed that the day-to-day business of the Ambanis did not appear to have been disturbed “even for a minute” after the incident. The court said there was nothing to show whether any member of the family even came to know that an explosives-laden vehicle had been parked near their residence. It also pointed out that no member of the Ambani family had lodged a complaint or given a statement during the investigation.Questioning NIA’s probe, the trial court said, “No one knows which Muhurat the investigating agency is waiting for to record statements of any of the targets of the alleged terror, after such a long gap of 5-6 years,” the court said. It added that the failure to record statements of the alleged targets was “precarious to the credibility of the prosecution case”.The NIA office is “literally just wall to wall adjacent” to Antilia the trial Judge said adding “this lassitude has to be seen with great pity and compassion”.In its appeal against the bail, NIA before the HC said the bail order was “eeroneous and ilegal’’ passed without going into detailed facts and circumstances and is “completely misplaced both, on facts and law.’’The NIA says, the special NIA court “completely ignored the rigours of section 43 D of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act while granting bail to the main accused (Waze) whose role is ‘central’ in character to the terror crime of this case.’’The NIA in its appeal said the “very substratum of the prosecution case is that, Waze after his reinstatement in police service after a long suspension, wanted to regain his clout’’ More over he was under the compelling circumstances to collect Rs 100 crore per month from hoteliers and bar owners in Mumbai and territory, and in that process, he intended huge monetary gain for himself also and for that hatched a criminal conspiracy with other accused in this case and committed all the alleged offences.’’You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Trump calls Sundar Pichai a 'monster' at White House event, Google CEO quips back
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump appeared to jokingly describe Google CEO Sundar Pichai as a “monster” during an event, before clarifying that he was referring
articles.body: US president Donald Trump appeared to jokingly describe Google CEO Sundar Pichai as a “monster” during an event, before clarifying that he was referring to Pichai’s stature and success.As Pichai began speaking, Trump said, “This guy is a monster, and nobody knows him. What a great life! To be a MONSTER and not have to go through this. All you have to know is — SUNDARR! Sundar is his name.”Pichai replied, “Hopefully a better tagline than I'm a monster!”This comes as US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a group of leading artificial intelligence company executives had signed a voluntary accord that includes internal and external reviews during a White House meeting aimed at addressing concerns over the technology.“I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson met with executives from major technology companies that are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in AI infrastructure, including data centres across the country. The projects have faced grassroots opposition from both Republicans and Democrats.The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX.Posted by Trump on Truth Social late Tuesday, the accord leaves open the possibility of future regulation while outlining four voluntary steps for the companies. It calls for “robust internal controls”, cooperation with an “independent external auditor” to assess those controls, and the creation of a committee within each company’s board to review reports from internal and external auditors.“Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said.Trump praised the executives for developing a technology he said would deliver “unbelievable growth”, while highlighting the economic impact of investment in data centres and related computer equipment.Amodei, who has been among the most outspoken voices calling for a slowdown in AI development, struck a more cautious note, saying, “The technology has very real risks.”"And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion,” Amodei said.You use AI every day. articles.summary: MANGALURU: A blast followed by a fire was reported at the CHT unit, the Hydro Sulphur Treatment Unit of Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL),
articles.body: MANGALURU: A blast followed by a fire was reported at the CHT unit, the Hydro Sulphur Treatment Unit of Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL), on Wednesday.The fire has since been brought under control, city police commissioner Sudheer Kumar Reddy CH said.One person, identified as Rajesh Baptist, sustained burn injuries covering around 35% of his body and was shifted to Srinivasa Hospital. He is undergoing treatment in the ICU and doctors said he is out of danger.Six other people who suffered minor injuries at an adjacent office were given outpatient treatment and underwent medical check-ups, police said.The city police commissioner, deputy commissioner and Zilla Panchayat CEO are present at the site. Police said there was no major cause for concern and that necessary precautionary measures were being taken.MRPL also confirmed that there were no casualties in the incident and appealed to people not to panic.The blast sent a loud boom across several kilometres, with thick black smoke billowing from the refinery premises. Residents of Jokatte and Surathkal reported that their houses shook and doors and windows vibrated following the explosion.The blast was also reportedly heard at Mangaluru airport, where windows of the administrative office rattled. Fire tenders and emergency teams were rushed to the refinery, while ambulances were seen leaving the premises.On the advice of the district administration, Mangaluru airport is conducting a visual inspection of vital installations in and around the airport, including the Precision Approach Lighting Category I systems and peripheral roads, to check their operational readiness.Dakshina Kannada MP Capt Brijesh Chowta said he was in constant touch with MRPL officials, the police commissioner and Fire and Emergency Services Department officials and was proceeding to the spot to assess the situation.He appealed to people to remain calm, refrain from spreading rumours or misinformation, and cooperate with the administration. articles.title: A farmer left $10.9 million to build a cancer centre; Mayo Clinic was supposed to get it only if the local hospital lost its independence
articles.summary: Iowa farmer Herman Carl Stille died in September 2020 at 94, leaving an estate worth about $10.9 million.
articles.body: Iowa farmer Herman Carl Stille died in September 2020 at 94, leaving an estate worth about $10.9 million. His 2017 will directed the remainder to Floyd County Medical Center (FCMC) in Charles City to establish a cancer centre for local residents. It also named the Mayo Foundation as the alternative recipient, for Alzheimer's research, if the hospital lost its independence and became part of a major healthcare corporation. Mayo went to court after the hospital found it could not provide radiation treatment. On May 1, 2026, the Iowa Supreme Court ruled in favour of the medical centre.A farmer's $10.9 million will with two conditionsStille was a cattle farmer and factory worker before he retired. He never married, had no children and left no living siblings or other identified heirs. He received care at FCMC for more than a decade and was the largest donor to the hospital's charitable foundation.He was also a Mayo patient in Rochester, Minnesota, and had given to its charitable foundation. His last gift there came in January 2017. He stopped donating because he was dissatisfied with the care he received, and his later gifts went to FCMC alone.The $10.9 million estate was mostly farmland. After several small charitable bequests, his will, signed in August 2017, gave the remainder to the hospital for a cancer centre. It required an oncologist on staff, office and consultation space, a family area and separate areas for radiation, chemotherapy and other treatments. The gift was contingent on the hospital staying independent. If it lost its independent status and joined a major healthcare corporation, the remainder would go to Mayo Foundation for Alzheimer's research.Attorney Michael Kennedy, who drafted the will, testified that Stille added the independence requirement in 2017. Stille's earlier will, from 2011, had no such condition and named Mayo as the backup only if the cancer centre could not be established. Stille's sister had died from Alzheimer's complications, and he feared facing the same disease.Radiation proved impossibleAfter Stille's death, FCMC began planning the centre, expecting roughly $10 million from the estate. Administrators soon realised they could not provide on-site radiation. Radiation requires a linear accelerator, which is costly and heavily regulated. In Iowa, a hospital needs a certificate of need, and one is generally not issued when radiation facilities already operate within a certain radius. Several hospitals near FCMC already offered radiation. The machine is also expensive to run, and FCMC lacked the patient base to afford its upkeep.The hospital said the centre could still satisfy the other requirements. It proposed to staff an oncologist through cooperation or subcontracting with other facilities, and to transport patients to another facility for radiation. It also noted that more cancer patients are treated with chemotherapy than with radiation.Mayo's challengeMayo asked the court to rule that the gift to FCMC had failed. It argued that the will's conditions went beyond independence, and that the money should pass to it if FCMC could not build the centre Stille described. Kennedy testified that Stille's intent was for the money to go to Mayo if either condition was unmet.FCMC countered that it had remained independent, so the trigger for Mayo's gift had never occurred.The Chickasaw County district court, after a three-day bench trial, ruled for FCMC in June 2025. It found that the hospital was independent and that its planned centre would meet five of the six specifications, all but radiation. The judge concluded that Stille cared more about the hospital's independence than about how the centre would operate, and would not have withdrawn the bequest had he known radiation was impossible.Iowa Supreme Court affirms on standingMayo appealed, and the Supreme Court retained the case. On May 1, 2026, it unanimously affirmed, in an opinion by Justice Thomas Waterman. Justice Mansfield took no part.The court did not adopt the district court's reasoning. It found no ambiguity in the will, which conditioned the gift to Mayo on FCMC's loss of independence. Because FCMC remained independent, and Mayo did not dispute that, the court held that Mayo takes nothing under the will. A beneficiary whose condition has not occurred lacks standing to challenge the gift to someone else, so the court affirmed on that basis alone and did not reach the remaining issues.The court noted that FCMC still has a legal and moral obligation to use the funds as intended. Mayo cannot enforce it, but the Iowa attorney general has standing to enforce the terms of charitable trusts.The ruling ends a dispute that began in 2021 and leaves the remainder of the $10.9 million estate with FCMC. The hospital says it will proceed with the Stille Cancer Centre on its campus. It says it is still unclear which cancer services will be available, including how radiation care will be provided for patients who need it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2005, two Vancouver writers ate only food produced within 100 miles to reconnect with local farms; they held the rule for a full year, with salt as the one exception
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking experiment, Vancouver writers Alisa Smith and J.B. MacKinnon committed to a 100-Mile Diet, consuming only local produce for a year. Their journey not only highlighted local food sources but also sparked a movement emphasizing sustainable eating practices.
articles.body: On March 21, 2005, Vancouver writers Alisa Smith and J.B. MacKinnon began a year-long experiment. They would buy food and drink for home consumption only if it had been produced within 100 miles of their Vancouver apartment. Grist reported that they completed the trial on March 20, 2006. The experiment drew heavy media attention. Grist reported that the couple's column about the 100-Mile Diet, first published on TheTyee.ca, attracted about 40,000 readers and was linked, reprinted and blogged about across the internet. "This is what it's like to witness the birth of a movement," MacKinnon said, and the couple soon launched the website 100MileDiet.org. Salt was the one known exception to their rule, and their book ends with a trip to Bamfield, where they boiled down seawater to make their own salt.The 100-mile rule, March 21, 2005 to March 20, 2006Their 100-mile circle was centered on their Vancouver apartment. The Tyee began publishing their series on June 28, 2005, and described it in a 2020 retrospective as a series that sparked a global phenomenon. The same retrospective noted that "locavore" was named 2007 Word of the Year by the New Oxford American Dictionary.Foods given up: sugar, Cheerios, olive oil, rice and beerThe book's description lists sugar, Cheerios, olive oil, rice, Pizza Pops and beer among the foods the couple did without. A 2008 Washington Post review of their memoir, Plenty, noted that they started with little gardening expertise, little money and little access to grocery stores selling local food. In a 2007 Grist interview, Smith said wheat was a big surprise for her. She explained that locally grown wheat flour was hard to find because wheat was traditionally grown on the West Coast before specialization shifted production to the prairie areas. Until they found locally milled flour, Smith said, they were unintentionally following the Atkins Diet.They made judgment calls about production methods. Smith said they accepted eggs from the UBC farm because they knew how the hens were raised and fed. MacKinnon said they accepted vegetables from non-organic growers after learning what the growers had applied and when. He also said local seafood was surprisingly difficult to obtain, despite their location at the mouth of a major salmon river. Even so, he called it the most varied year of eating either of them had ever had.Salt was the one item in their cabinets that did not come from what they called home. The Last Bastille's review noted that the first meal described in the book had only one non-local ingredient, salt from a bag from Oregon, several hundred miles away. In a 2020 interview with The Tyee, MacKinnon said the story ends with a visit to Bamfield, where they boiled seawater to make salt, and that he would now buy salt from Vancouver Island Salt Co. in Black Creek.Food-miles study, 2008: transport 11 percent of emissions, production 83 percentThe study Food-Miles and the Relative Climate Impacts of Food Choices in the United States, published in Environmental Science & Technology in 2008, reported that food travels 1,640 kilometers (1,020 miles) on average for final delivery and 6,760 kilometers across the life-cycle supply chain. Even so, production accounted for 83 percent of the average American household's food-related greenhouse gas emissions. Transportation as a whole made up 11 percent, and final delivery from producer to retail only 4 percent.The authors found that shifting less than one day per week's worth of calories from red meat and dairy products to chicken, fish, eggs or a vegetable-based diet would cut more emissions than buying all food locally. The research covered the average American household, not Smith and MacKinnon specifically. Grist noted that the diet began as an effort to reduce dependence on the fossil fuels used by the conventional food system, then grew into an exploration of community, seasons and flavor.USDA report, 2010: no generally accepted definition of local foodThe USDA Economic Research Service report Local Food Systems: Concepts, Impacts, and Issues found no generally accepted definition of local in terms of the distance between production and consumption. The report also found that local food systems made up only a tiny fraction of US agricultural output, even though their share was growing. It noted that small farmers earned more from direct-to-consumer sales than larger farmers did, and it found conflicting evidence on local food's contribution to development, nutrition and greenhouse gas reductions.Direct sales from farmers to consumers made up only 0.4 percent of all agricultural sales in 2007, a narrow measure of local food. The report identified limits to the sector's growth, including the small capacity of farms and the lack of systems to deliver local foods to traditional markets. Its evidence on the effects of local food on the economy, health and nutrition was inconsistent.After March 2006: farmers' markets, a community garden plot and winter preservingGrist reported that after the year the couple planned to keep shopping at farmers' markets, tend their community garden plot and preserve local produce for the winter. MacKinnon said their first meal after the experiment was potatoes and eggs, and that they went out for Indian food later that night. Beer, chocolate, olives, lemons and olive oil returned to their diet, but he said some of the foods they had given up did not come back.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2017, a California wildlife-park owner defied a wildfire evacuation to protect 1,000 animals; by morning, he had lost no animal, bird or structure
articles.summary: In an incredible act of bravery during the devastating 2017 wildfires, Safari West owner Peter Lang defied evacuation orders to protect over 1,000 animals, saving them all amid chaos.
articles.body: On the night of Sunday, October 8, 2017, a wildfire closed in on Safari West, a wildlife preserve near Santa Rosa in Sonoma County, and its 77-year-old owner, Peter Lang, remained there after officials ordered an evacuation. KQED reported that Lang said officials wanted everyone to evacuate and that he could not leave. Lang worked late into the night fighting small fires amid 1,000 animals or more. He stated that by dawn, he hadn't lost a single animal, bird, or building at the preserve, even though his own house had burned down a mile down the road. That account comes from Lang himself and has not been independently audited.Evacuation order at Safari West, night of October 8, 2017According to The Washington Times, the preserve had emergency plans for earthquakes, floods and wildfires, including fires that could arrive with as little as three hours' notice, but officers arrived on Sunday night and gave the workers only 15 minutes to evacuate. The Visit California profile describes how Lang evacuated his wife, guests and employees, then stayed behind to defend the preserve. Alone on the grounds, he connected hoses to put out spot fires that started when embers fell into the grass. KQED reported that he also had to drive cornered nyala antelope through a ring of fire.The preserve's animals: about 1,000 across 98 species, 2017The Washington Times reported that the preserve housed about 1,000 animals of 98 species, and Visit California listed giraffes, cheetahs, rhinoceroses and hyenas among them. Later sources give slightly different figures, but these numbers describe the preserve in October 2017. Lang bought the former ranch in the 1980s and turned it into a wildlife preserve. According to Visit California, he and his zoologist wife, Nancy, started a captive breeding program, and the preserve opened to visitors in 1993. The Washington Times also reported that about 150 employees worked at the preserve and at least 11 of them lost their homes in the fires.Lang's report: no animals or structures lost, home a mile away destroyedLang, according to KQED, said that he had not lost any animal, any bird and any building, but he lost his house. On the day when the evacuation took place, Lang was at home with his wife one mile away from the reserve. The aviary was the most vulnerable of all buildings. Lang told KQED that if a burning branch had fallen on the aviary, it would have burned down. Some of the employees were able to get inside despite the fact that there was a power outage. Fred Dickerson, one of the employees, told KQED that they were able to account for every animal, even those that they released for flying. Fox News reported that Safari West posted on Facebook that its fences were still intact and that all animals were contained, accounted for and safe. KQED also reported that after the fire, Lang and his wife called the park their home.NIST case study, 2007 Witch Fire: 74 of 245 homes destroyed in The TrailsThe National Institute of Standards and Technology examined a community affected by two 2007 fires in its report, A Case Study of a Community Affected by the Witch and Guejito Fires. The community, The Trails in Rancho Bernardo north of San Diego, had 274 homes, 245 of them within the fire perimeter. Of those, 74 were completely destroyed and 16 were partly damaged, according to NIST. The report describes ember attack, both direct and indirect, as a contributing factor in the destruction of homes in the community, and NIST's summary said embers ignited about two-thirds of the destroyed homes. The report notes that defensive measures had been taken at about one-third of the houses and that 15 of the 16 partly damaged houses had been successfully defended.California Agriculture survey, 2025: 505 producers, 65 percent sheltered in place or defended propertyThe study Farming and ranching through wildfire: Producers' critical role in fire risk management and emergency response, published in California Agriculture in 2025, surveyed 505 California farmers and ranchers affected by wildfires between 2017 and 2023. Sixty-five percent of producers said they sheltered in place or defended their property at least once when a wildfire approached. Of those who evacuated, 75 percent returned as soon as possible to assess and reduce damage.Among the 146 livestock producers surveyed, 32 percent said they had to evacuate their livestock. The authors noted that evacuation can protect animals but can also add to their stress and health problems. In addition, 77 percent of the 303 producers near wildfires gave direct support to neighbors and emergency responders, and 47 percent said that support included creating firebreaks and defending properties directly.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Virginia woman paid $3.99 for a vase at Goodwill; after experts identified it as a rare 1940s Carlo Scarpa Murano work, months later, the rare vase sold for $107,100
articles.summary: It started like any ordinary day. On a June afternoon, Jessica Vincent, 43, was browsing the shelves of a Virginia thrift store.
articles.body: It started like any ordinary day. On a June afternoon, Jessica Vincent, 43, was browsing the shelves of a Virginia thrift store. That’s when a striking vase caught her eye. The bottle-shaped vase had ribbons of colours, aqua green and amethyst purple, spiralled up its glass surface like stripes of paint.On its base, there were two words: ‘Murano’ and ‘Italia’.Vincent, a horse trainer, didn’t think twice about buying the vase. She paid $3.99 for it at a Goodwill. "I bought it thinking it would look beautiful in my house somewhere," she told the Associated Press.One lucky findVincent has been visiting thrift stores since she was a child. She accompanied her mother to second-hand stores, yard sales and flea markets. In fact, she loves thrifting so much that she goes to thrift stores a few times a week with her partner, Naza Acosta. She is obsessed with PBS’ ‘Antiques Roadshow’ and has long daydreamed about a lottery-ticket find.So when she found a beautiful vase, she went for it. The vase felt heavy in her hands. Though she had seen painted glass before, the colour grabbed her eyeballs. “I always felt like I had a good eye. But I’m really surprised that nobody picked it up before I did,” she told the outlet. But she had no plans to flip it when buying it. “I definitely didn’t buy it thinking, ‘Oh, I’m going to sell this.’”After reading Murano’s name on the vase, she posted photos on Facebook groups for glass art. She also joined a private group for Murano collectors. And one reply stopped her cold. She learned that those pieces are very rare. “Those are very rare. Every collector would love to have that. But most people cannot afford them,” one Facebook user told her.Finding such a rare piece also surprised the thrift store managers. Laura Faison, a spokeswoman for Goodwill of Central and Coastal Virginia, told the outlet the vase probably sat on the shelf for only a couple of days. Each store handles about 2,000 new pieces daily, many arriving from car trunks. "It could have been someone cleaning out grandma's basement," Faison said. "We'll probably never know."The Murano written on the bottom of the vase referred to an island in Venice that has been famous for its glasswork since the 13th century. Some of its highly priced pieces include ornate crystal chandeliers and mirror frames, many of which adorn the palaces of Europe’s aristocracy.This particular vase was produced by the famous glass company Venini and designed by Italian architect Carlo Scarpa, who died in 1978.Selling the $3.99 vase for $107,100Vincent was pointed to Richard Wright, president of the Wright Auction House in Chicago. He recognised the piece the moment her email arrived. “The minute I saw her email, I knew what it was and how rare it was.”Scarpa, a top Italian glass designer from the mid-20th century, designed this vase as part of a series created in 1942. The collection was called Pennellate, which means brushstroke, and was made by adding coloured opaque glass to the vase as it was blown.“It was basically a duet between Carlo Scarpa and a master blower who had to physically translate (Scarpa’s) drawings. You have to keep rotating this vase the entire time or it’ll slump off the pipe. While at the same time you’re applying these delicate brushes of colour that have this absolute lightness to them,” Wright explained.Only a few such vases were created because they were very difficult to make. The auction house, of course, knew its value. On Dec. 13, 2023, the vase was sold through the Wright Auction House for $107,100. The buyer is a top collector from Europe who wished to remain private. It went into the buyer’s private collection.Vincent hopes the vase will someday land in a museum, so she can catch a glimpse of it once more. “My little 1930s farmhouse is not the right showcase for something so spectacular. It would also make me super nervous to have it in my house. It’s a lot of responsibility when you find out how much something is worth.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2018, Malibu residents stayed after a mandatory evacuation during the Woolsey Fire; their volunteer group was credited with saving dozens of homes
articles.summary: In the 2018 Woolsey Fire, Malibu residents, through their volunteer group 'Point Dume Bombers', remained behind during mandatory evacuations and played a crucial role in saving dozens of homes. Discover the impact of community cooperation and preparedness in wildfire situations.
articles.body: Leave as soon as an evacuation order is issued. One of the most well-known instances was the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Malibu, California, which influenced how one of the country’s largest fire agencies views residents who stay behind. The fire began on Nov. 8, 2018, near the Santa Susana Field Laboratory above Simi Valley, close to the Los Angeles-Ventura County line, and reached Malibu early the next day. The Los Angeles County After Action Review documented the combination of factors, the rapid spread over the 101 motorway, and a warning to the public that agencies will not always be immediately available. At the time, a volunteer group of homeowners known as the Point Dume Bomberos remained behind after the required evacuation and battled spot fires, and neighbours credited them with helping protect homes in the area.Why neighbours stayed inThe Woolsey Fire burnt 96,949 acres and destroyed 1,643 structures, according to California state records. Three people were killed. A mandatory evacuation order was issued for all of Malibu on Nov. 9, yet as the fire tore through the hills, some residents questioned whether enough fire resources were available.The county review helps explain why the official response was stretched. The review said the Woolsey Fire struck while the Camp Fire was raging in Northern California, and other emergencies were drawing from the same limited pool of firefighting resources. That contributed to delays in getting large numbers of engines into Malibu. The study also pointed out deficiencies in communicating evacuations to the public.Some residents said their knowledge of the local streets and terrain helped them understand where fires were developing and where they needed help. For others on Point Dume, a headland most people never thought to burn, that vista proved costly.Even with volunteers on the ground, the fire drew close. About 90 homes were lost on the Point, roughly 15% of its 610 properties, The Malibu Times reported.Inside the volunteer pushThe group took its name from an older Point Dume surf team known as the Bombers. A phone call among surfing friends brought together about 15 people within hours, and as the days passed, the number climbed to some 2. They used hand tools, a water truck and dirt motorcycles and walkie-talkies to stay in touch when phone coverage failed. One of the organizers prepared a map and, using binoculars from a lookout point, spotted flare-ups and radioed the others with their approximate locations.One member, Sam McGee, told CNN the crew put out at least 100 hot spots in five days and got nine hours of sleep out of 144. McGee also cautioned against taking all the credit, saying that luck helped some residences. He said there were no further structure fires after the first bad night. Local accounts credited the group with helping protect homes from spot fires and flare-ups.Fire science can help explain why such patrols may be important. A USDA Forest Service report by US Forest Service scientist Jack Cohen discovered that the large flames of strong wildfires don’t immediately ignite homes beyond 100 feet. The ignitions are from things close to the house, mainly smouldering embers and small surface fires that are igniting items close to the house. A house can survive a fire that passes at full strength if there is someone to smother the little ember fire on a deck or in a gutter.Their support was more than just firefighting. The same group also helped bring in food and water when the road was closed and supplies were running low, and later they ran a relief facility in a school car park near Point Dume. Members of the Bombers also decided that the experience should not depend on luck next time.The brigade model that came afterA 2026 report from the Natural Hazards Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, Trial by Fire, examined the Community Brigade pilot during the first seven days of the December 2024 Franklin Fire and January 2025 Palisades Fire in Malibu. Based on participant observations and interviews with brigade members and officials, the researchers reported preliminary evidence of greater trust, fire-risk awareness and community ownership.The report also distinguished between the two models. Community brigade volunteers undergo extensive training under the direction of the county fire department and the US Forest Service and are called into service when needed. That is unlike stay-at-home defenders who reject evacuation orders. Trained and coordinated volunteers bring local expertise to a professional response, whereas untrained residents who refuse to leave put themselves and the personnel that may have to rescue them in danger.For Malibu, the experience points to the value of preparation before a fire starts. Residents are still urged to evacuate when ordered, while organized community brigades can help share information, support evacuation and reduce ember-related risks under official direction. Homes with fewer combustible materials around them are better positioned to withstand wildfire, while communities that train and coordinate before an emergency are better prepared to respond safely.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, a California homeowner refused to leave as the Creek Fire closed in; he and his son kept flames from reaching their house, which was left standing
articles.summary: A gripping story of survival as a California homeowner and his son protect their house from the devastating Creek Fire through determination, preparation, and bravery. Discover the strategies they used to combat smaller flames and save their home while others were lost.
articles.body: Within minutes, a wildfire can alter the surroundings of a house. Strong winds and exceptionally dry conditions drove the Creek Fire through the foothills north of Los Angeles on December 5, 2017. Burning embers were carried ahead of the main fire and ignited secondary fires around buildings, endangering homes in and around Kagel Canyon.A neighbour warned Wood Grigsby, who had lived in upper Kagel Canyon for about 12 years, about the fire while he was asleep. When he got outdoors, he discovered that surrounding properties were already in danger and that flames were spreading throughout the canyon. In contrast to nearby properties, his house was somewhat protected. Grigsby had cleared brush around the house and replaced some vegetation with gravel, reducing the fuel immediately surrounding the property.As the fire advanced, Grigsby and his son started to move furniture off the porch and look for embers and spot fires. As surrounding homes burnt, they spent hours fighting tiny fires around the property. One house was demolished about 180 feet up the hill from Grigsby’s dwelling. The Creek Fire burnt 15,619 acres in Los Angeles County and destroyed 123 structures, including 60 homes, according to CAL FIRE figures reported the week it burned.How the fire came to the neighbourhoodThe blaze began at about 3:44 a.m. near Kagel Canyon, in the Angeles National Forest area, and grew during a time of extreme wildfire weather. in Southern California, when high winds may quickly spread fires through dry vegetation and carry burning material over the region. But for those who lived in the canyon, the threat wasn't only the main wall of fire. As foliage and structures were burnt, it generated embers that might be blown through the air and land on properties some distance distant. These embers can then spark fires in grass, leaves, landscaping material, fences or other combustibles.Those small fires matter because wildfire researchers have found that homes can catch fire through several different channels. A dwelling need not be located in the primary fire front. Research by the National Institute of Standards and Technology found that firebrands, or smouldering embers, can ignite mulch near a structure, depending on their size and number, airflow, and the moisture of the material. Researchers looked at firebrands, or smouldering embers, and how they can ignite fires in mulch near structures. Their investigations demonstrated that igniting depended on the size and number of firebrands, airflow and the moisture level of the material. Once the spark ignites a tiny fire close to a house, the risk might rise quickly. A burning piece of landscaping material could send flames to siding, decks or other combustible portions of a building.Why some homes did not burnOne big benefit Grigsby had before the fire came was that there was less flammable foliage just around the house. He'd cut the undergrowth surrounding the place and put in gravel instead of letting the plants grow right up against the building. So when embers landed, they had fewer fuels to catch fire with and travel to the structure. This form of planning is frequently referred to as constructing defensible space. The underlying principle is to eliminate as many flammable items around the house as possible, reducing the likelihood of the fire and embers coming into contact with the structure.A 2019 study by Alexandra Syphard and USGS scientist Jon Keeley, published in the journal Fire, offers wider context. The researchers analysed building inspectors' reports for more than 40,000 wildfire-exposed structures across California between 2013 and 2018, comparing homes that survived with those destroyed. Statewide, structural characteristics explained more of the difference than defensible-space distance did, though destroyed homes were over-represented in the dataThe most consistently important features were enclosed eaves, vent screens and multi-pane windows. These elements may reduce the chance of wind-borne embers entering a building. Multi-pane windows can also provide added protection from radiant heat. The authors also noted a limitation: many homes with more than 30 metres of defensible space or fire-resistant materials were still destroyed. That means no single preparedness step will ensure a house survives a big wildfire.Embers can convert a little fire into a house fire.Controlled wildfire studies further highlight the importance of material right adjacent to a home. In a separate NIST investigation, scientists tested several types of mulch beside realistic-scale building corners and exposed the area to showers of firebrands. The experiments found that firebrands could first create smouldering ignition in mulch, which could then transition to flaming. Under the tested wind conditions, flames from the burning mulch eventually ignited the adjacent building assembly.The results help explain why the few feet around a house can be so important in a wildfire. A fire doesn’t have to look like a single big flame front. An ember can fall on a flammable item, ignite it and then offer the following step towards the building. Grigsby and his son weren't trying to stop the fire; they were guarding against exactly this kind of ember ignition. But Grigsby's story is not to suggest that homeowners should stay and fight an advancing wildfire. Conditions near a fire can change rapidly, and skilled firefighters risk a lot even with training, protective equipment and communication systems.The greater lesson from his house’s survivalWhat made Grigsby’s experience remarkable was that his house survived as homes around him burnt. But the fact of one house cannot be reduced to one deed. The state of the property before the fire was significant. The house's structure was important. The wind direction and the severity of the fire also played a part, as did the behaviour of embers and the presence or absence of flammable material surrounding the structure.A USGS study supports that point. In their analysis, structural traits were a crucial factor in explaining which California homes survived. But the researchers also observed that the criteria they analysed could not account for all structural loss. Thus, Grigsby’s efforts during the fire represented only one part of the story. Vegetation clearance ahead of time to reduce fuel and gravel made a less flammable surface. Moving furniture away from the house removed another probable ignition source. The Creek Fire demonstrated how a neighbourhood can swiftly become a series of distinct fire environments. One property burns, while another adjacent one survives. An ember falling harmlessly on gravel can ignite a hazardous fire on dry grass or combustible landscaping.Their home remained standingThe bigger lesson is not that householders can safely fight a wildfire on their own. The wildfire survival starts before the flames arrive. Building design, ember resistance, vegetation management and removal of flammable debris can influence what happens when a wind-driven fire hits a town. Grigsby's house was one of those that survived, a reminder that a wildfire's effect on a home depends on more than whether flames reach the building.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Jiya Joshi was rejected from volunteering at a nursing home at 14; she later built a lifesaving 500-student senior care movement
articles.summary: Jiya Joshi lost her beloved grandmother at 14 and decided to volunteer at a nursing home.
articles.body: Jiya Joshi lost her beloved grandmother at 14 and decided to volunteer at a nursing home. But getting rejected from there inspired her to begin a movement uniting generations through friendship, compassion and caring.A love lost too soonJiya was only two when her grandparents arrived from India to Texas, to help care for her while her parents were at work. Her grandmother, Saroj, drove her to school and cooked her the most delicious snacks. Her entire day was wrapped around them and the two formed a close bond, sharing long conversations about life, school and friends.When she was in third grade, her grandparents returned to India, but distance only made the heart grow fonder, and they spoke on the phone regularly once a week.The year she turned 14, Jiya lost her grandmother, whom she called 'Dadi' and the loss left an aching void inside her, often leaving her feeling lonely. While she had her parents and friends to talk to, it wasn't the same. They didn't carry the same wisdom and gentle kindness as her grandmother did.Filling the voidThis is when an idea struck. “What if I visit a nursing home? Maybe the residents would enjoy a visit as much as I would?” she asked. Jiya decided to volunteer at a nursing home and after being put on hold several times, she finally reached the nursing home volunteer coordinator: "I want to volunteer and visit," she explained, as per a report by Woman's World.The administrator was welcoming until she learnt Jiya was only 14. “We don’t allow volunteers under 18,” she declared. “Our staff doesn’t have time to care for both children and our seniors.”Jiya's heart was crushed, and not just due to the rejection. There was also the lingering grief of having lost one of her favourite people in the world, her Dadi. After several more refusals to volunteer, she decided to do something different.“Could I come just once — a trial visit?” she asked Sharon Williams, Activities Director at Houston’s Landon Ridge Assisted Living. “If it doesn’t work, I won’t bother you again.” Williams was touched by the girl's sincerity and decided to agree. "Let's give it a try," she said and Jiya was over the moon.Jiya arrived for her first visit at the centre with a box of supplies. She approached a group of seniors in a recreation area, put on a bright smile and introduced herself. “I’m Jiya. Would you like to paint with me?” “I love painting!” exclaimed a woman named Betty and soon she was regaling Jiya with incredible tales of her years as a nurse in Vietnam.“I was a pilot fighting the Germans in World War II,” said a second resident, and a third rushed off and returned with a chunk of concrete. “You mentioned Germany; this is part of the Berlin Wall, a piece of history,” she explained.As the word of a youthful stranger spread, residents who rarely left their rooms came out to see what the excitement was about. By the end of her visit, Jiya had made a dozen new friends and spread even more smiles. “I’ve never seen them so active,” Sharon marvelled as she helped Jiya pack up. “You’re coming back, right?”Jiya returned every Saturday that summer. While the residents loved having such a lively young person around to hold conversation and company with, Jiya loved their stories and affectionate hugs.A generational movementWhen school started again, Jiya invited her friends to join her and many of them said yes. The teens visited in pairs and after a few outings, many told Jiya, "This is the most fun I've had volunteering."It was one invitation from Betty that caught her by surprise. "Betty asked me to keep her company at the senior home’s 4th of July event because she did not have any family to eat with her at the event," Jiya shared. This is when she thought about how many seniors were in need of active company. Roughly one in four Americans aged 65 and older is socially isolated, and 30–35% of seniors report feeling lonely at least some of the time. This isolation is linked to serious health risks, including higher rates of depression, heart disease, stroke, and cognitive decline.As interest spread, Jiya founded a youth-led non-profit organisation, Young and Old United, a movement that allowed teens to volunteer at elder care facilities while spreading love and support among hundreds of seniors across Houston.Generations were united through the feelings of friendship, compassion and care. Within two years of service, Jiya has helped 4,000 seniors, built a network of more than 70 youth volunteers and spread the initiative in more than 11 countries through an ambassador program. Together, they have raised $9,000 through local fundraisers and grants and partnered with dentists to obtain dental kits to include in hygiene kits.Hundreds of middle and high school students have begun making regular nursing home visits across the state. She mobilises youth volunteers to assemble and personally deliver hygiene kits to isolated and underrepresented seniors, offer spa days to senior women, and conduct senior interviews. YOU has also won thousands of dollars in grants from Youth Service America, AmeriCorps, and H.E.B and has an ongoing partnership with staff from United Airlines, providing hygiene kits.“Their eyes light up when they see her coming,” said Sharon. "My grandmother was a bright personality. She was a safe space where I could talk about anything. Then, when she left my life, I sought to regain the strongest connection I had ever built by reaching out to seniors within my own neighbourhood," Jiya told Bold Journey.“Our seniors still have so much to offer,” Jiya insists. “My grandmother taught me that. I can feel her smiling down on me!”Jiya hopes to help more than 3000+ seniors in 2026.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 2 Indians charged in US for smuggling fake Ozempic from China
articles.summary: The Justice Department has charged two Indian nationals for smuggling counterfeit Ozempic, a weight-loss drug, into the US from China, putting consumers at risk.
articles.body: Two Indian nationals have been charged in the United States for allegedly smuggling counterfeit Ozempic, a weight-loss drug, from China and selling the products to distributors in the country, the Department of Justice said Tuesday.Swapnadip Roy, 33, and Vicky Ramancha, 37, were charged in the Middle District of Florida. Roy was extradited from Italy to the US and made his initial appearance in Tampa on Tuesday, where he pleaded not guilty. Ramancha remains at large.Prosecutors allege that Roy and Ramancha obtained counterfeit Ozempic in China between July 2023 and April 2024 and sold the products to US distributors at discounted prices.The counterfeit products allegedly included packaging, package inserts, pen labels and needles designed to make buyers believe they were purchasing genuine Ozempic authorised by the manufacturer.The alleged scheme continued even after the US Food and Drug Administration seized some of the counterfeit Ozempic in December 2023 and issued a public warning about the products, the department said.Roy and Ramancha are charged with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and defraud the United States, three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale.If convicted, each faces a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison.Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division said counterfeit prescription drugs pose a threat to people who depend on the safety of the pharmaceutical supply.“These defendants allegedly exploited people’s health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs,” Duva said.Assistant US Attorney Christopher Murray for the Middle District of Florida said the indictment reflected the department's efforts to protect Americans from potential harm caused by counterfeit prescription drugs.The FDA's Office of Criminal Investigations is investigating the case. Assistant Commissioner Justin Green said introducing counterfeit drugs into the US pharmaceutical supply chain puts consumers at significant risk.Roy was arrested in Italy pursuant to an INTERPOL Red Notice before the Justice Department secured his continued detention and sought his extradition to the US.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, 11 zoo workers rode out Hurricane Ian at Central Florida Zoo, staying around the clock so every animal continued to receive care through the storm
articles.summary: A dedicated team of 11 zoo workers remained on-site at Central Florida Zoo during Hurricane Ian, ensuring the safety and care of over 400 animals while facing severe storm conditions.
articles.body: When a hurricane threatens a zoo, staff can choose whether to evacuate. The animals can't, and they still need food, warmth and veterinary care during a storm. Many zoos keep a small ride-out crew on site during storms. In September 2022, the Central Florida Zoo and Botanical Gardens in Sanford put that strategy to the test. According to the zoo, from Wednesday through Friday, a team of 11 animal care, veterinary and facility professionals from the Central Florida Zoo remained at the zoo 24 hours a day. The outcome was successful, all the animals and crew stayed safe, although the storm caused heavy damage around the grounds. The episode shows how preparation and a small on-site crew can protect animals during a hurricane.Inside the ride-out crewIt was a team of mixed skills, and that counted. "Zookeepers fed and cared for the animals daily, veterinary staff stood by for any medical problems, and the facilities crew maintained the buildings and grounds. The zoo, home to more than 400 animals, closed to visitors on September 28, the day Ian made landfall on Florida's west coast.Preparation had begun days earlier. The animal care staff is getting additional food and medication and moving it to locations that won't flood," Christopher Torge, the zoo's head of animal operations, said ahead of the storm. The veterinary staff confirmed that zookeepers had all the medicines they would need, and the nutrition crew arranged meals to last several days. ABC News reported that the birds were kenneled and moved to a safe building where the crew would also shelter, with extra food, blankets and toys to keep them calm.The zoo said in its statement that all of its animals had safe, secure quarters to ride-out the storm and that every bird was brought indoors for extra protection. That routine work can make the difference between safety and disaster.What Hurricane Ian did to SanfordIan was a wild tempest even when far from where it initially made landfall. The National Hurricane Center said it made landfall in southwestern Florida as a Category 4 hurricane and caused record freshwater flooding across much of central and northern Florida. Its assessment says Ian damaged 1,656 structures in Seminole County, home of the zoo, and more than 250 water rescues in central and eastern Florida.Zoo officials who walked the grounds Friday found fallen trees, damaged fences, two buildings with water damage and debris in the walkways. The Wayne M. Densch Discovery Center suffered the worst damage, with water bubbling up from bathroom drains and storm water forcing its way into the back of the building. Repairs were estimated to take a month or more.The greater surprise came days later. Stormwater flowed towards Lake Monroe and started rising rapidly Sunday night, and by Monday morning the only road in and out of the zoo was overflowing. That morning, managers sent non-essential staff and volunteers home and devised a plan to ferry essential workers in and out each day to tend to the animals, including a second ride-out team if one became necessary. From then on, Glover said, staff were on site every day, even when the water made the road impassable. The zoo reopened on October 26 after a four-week closure, and CEO Richard Glover estimated damage and operating costs at more than $800,000.Why zoos plan like thisThe vast majority of zoos do not evacuate their animals, and there are good reasons for this. Because hurricanes can change direction at the last minute, transferring animals can mean driving them right into a more dangerous spot, Zoo Miami explained. The stress of transit can be more dangerous than staying in a secure building during the storm. The safer way is to bolster the housing and keep the people with the animals.Past calamities have also helped shape planning. A US Department of Agriculture gap analysis of zoo and aquarium resilience in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 revealed that facilities with pre-catastrophe action plans did better and recovered more, according to the AZA, the Association of Zoos and Aquariums.Other zoos do things that way. In Houston, the Houston Zoo had 15 team members on site the first night of Hurricane Harvey, sleeping on cots on the floor and using radios to ensure every animal had the correct feed, NPR reported. At Central Florida Zoo, staff also faced damage and losses at home but put the animals first, CEO Richard Glover said in an October 7 note. That part of the story is harder to capture in a checklist.The Sanford example shows how ride-out crews work in practice. The flooding that followed kept the zoo closed, but every animal stayed safe. Storms can only be anticipated so far, which is why zoos rely on preparation and a small crew willing to stay.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Pilot stabbed, blood in cockpit: Passengers recall harrowing ordeal on Flydubai flight that nearly crashed
articles.summary: Passengers aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv described scenes of panic in the air after screams erupted on board, a pilot was reportedly
articles.body: Passengers aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv described scenes of panic in the air after screams erupted on board, a pilot was reportedly stabbed and the Boeing 737 MAX suddenly went into a steep dive before eventually making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.“We heard screams on the plane. Then they opened the cockpit and we saw blood, and someone had stabbed the pilot with a pocket knife,” an Israeli passenger told Channel 12, describing the moments after the incident broke out.Another passenger, who identified herself as Noam was quoted by Times of Israel, stating passengers realised something was wrong as the screams spread through the cabin.“Screams began on the plane… by passengers who realized what was happening,” she said, adding that they understood one of the pilots had been stabbed and seriously wounded and that the aircraft had lost control and begun to dive rapidly.The passengers said some Israelis on board helped crew members restrain the attacker. One passenger recalled that there were moments when those on board believed they might not survive.A separate report by Channel 12 said there were two additional pilots travelling as passengers on the flight, dressed in civilian clothes.According to the report, the pilots helped prevent one of the flight's pilots from taking control of the aircraft and were among the passengers who intervened during the confrontation.A senior Israeli official told Channel 12 that without the presence of the additional pilots, the incident could have ended in another September 11, 2001, attack or an Entebbe-style hostage incident.The report has not been independently confirmed.Separately, news agency Walla reported that the pilot under investigation is Omani.READ ALSO: Russia raises active troop numbers to 1.55 million as Zelensky accuses Kremlin of mass mobilisationPlane suddenly plunged thousands of feetThe flight, FDB1073, was carrying around 180 passengers, including dozens of Israelis, when it declared an emergency while flying over the Jordan-Saudi Arabia border.The Boeing 737 MAX initially transmitted the international emergency code 7700 before briefly sending code 7500, which indicates hijacking or unlawful interference. Israeli authorities scrambled fighter jets as they were unable to establish contact with the aircraft.Publicly available flight data showed the aircraft suddenly dropping from about 34,000 feet to around 17,000 feet in less than a minute, while its speed rose sharply. It then climbed briefly before dropping again to below 14,000 feet. For the following hour, the aircraft struggled to maintain a steady altitude.The aircraft eventually established contact and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said all passengers were safe and accounted for, while declining to provide further details beyond confirming that an incident had occurred.What happened inside the cockpit?Israeli officials said the emergency signals appeared to have been triggered after a fight broke out between the two pilots, although the precise circumstances had not been confirmed by flydubai. Passengers reported blood in the cockpit and said one of the pilots had been stabbed.There were also unconfirmed reports, based on passenger testimony, that one pilot had attempted to crash the aircraft as a suicide attempt and was stopped by the other pilot with help from passengers.A senior Israeli official later told Channel 12 that a “major disaster” had been averted and said the copilot was being investigated amid indications that he had attempted to take control of the aircraft in order to crash it.The investigation is ongoing, and the circumstances surrounding the cockpit altercation have yet to be fully established.You use AI every day. articles.body: A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an incident on board, with reports pointing to an altercation between the two pilots.Israeli fighter jets were scrambled amid initial fears of a possible hijacking, while the aircraft later landed safely in Tabuk.The exact circumstances remain under investigation, and several details reported by Israeli media have not been independently confirmed by the airline or authorities.What happened on the flight?Flydubai flight FZ 1073 was travelling from Dubai International Airport to Ben Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv when it experienced what the airline described only as an "incident".The aircraft landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia, and flydubai said all passengers were safe and accounted for.“Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities,” the airline said. “Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available.”According to publicly available flight-tracking data cited by news agency AFP, the aircraft suddenly descended from nearly 34,000 feet to less than 17,000 feet within about a minute.Israeli media reported that an emergency signal was transmitted and that a fight had apparently broken out between the pilots. The exact cause of the altercation has not been confirmed.What is being reported about the pilot?According to the Times of Israel, citing the Walla news outlet, the pilot under investigation is Omani.As per Channel 12, a second team of pilots in civilian clothes was travelling as passengers on the aircraft. According to the report, they helped prevent one of the pilots from taking control of the aircraft.Israeli media have further reported that authorities are investigating whether one of the pilots attempted to crash the plane. Channel 12 said authorities were examining whether one pilot had attempted a possible suicide by trying to crash the aircraft, with the other pilot apparently intervening.These reports remain unconfirmed. Neither flydubai nor authorities involved in the incident have provided details on what happened inside the cockpit.What did passengers report?Passengers told Israeli media that they heard screams and noticed a sudden descent of the aircraft.One passenger told Israeli media that passengers heard screams before the cockpit was opened and that blood was visible inside. She said Israeli passengers helped crew members restrain the attacker.Another passenger, identified as Noam, told Channel 12 that passengers realised something was wrong after hearing screams.“Screams began on the plane, by passengers who realised what was happening. We understand that one of the pilots was stabbed and seriously wounded, and they lost control of the plane. It started to dive quickly. It was very scary,” she said.Israeli media, citing anonymous sources, published photographs of a passenger wearing a bloodied T-shirt.ALSO READ: Hijacking scare on Dubai-Tel Aviv flight; emergency code triggered, plane diverted to Saudi ArabiaWhy were Israeli fighter jets scrambled?Israeli media reported that fighter jets were sent to intercept the aircraft after concerns about a possible hijacking. However, the hypothesis was later dismissed.The Israeli Prime Minister's Office said Benjamin Netanyahu held consultations after concerns over the aviation incident and was monitoring developments.“The incident is under control, and all measures are currently being deployed in order to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel,” it said.The aircraft was later confirmed to have landed safely in Tabuk.What happens next?The incident remains under investigation. Flydubai said its teams were working with the relevant authorities and that further updates would be issued once confirmed information became available.The airline was also sending another aircraft to Tabuk to transport the stranded passengers to Tel Aviv.You use AI every day. articles.title: US completes military withdrawal from Iraq after years of operations
articles.summary: The 12-year effort to combat, the Islamic state organization came to an end on Wednesday, when the US military declared that all of its forces had left
articles.body: The 12-year effort to combat, the Islamic state organization came to an end on Wednesday, when the US military declared that all of its forces had left Iraq. According to an agreement between Baghdad and Washington, American soldiers finally departed an air base in northern Iraq.The evacuation, which was decided upon two years ago, takes place in the context of the continuous conflict between the United States and Iran, which has occasionally spilled over into Iraq, with the United States attacking the militias' strongholds and Iran-backed militias shooting on American forces.Baghdad celebrated the US mission's termination as an indication of the nation's growing might and independence.Iran-backed organizations also applauded the evacuation, while some other Iraqis, especially those in the Kurdish area, expressed alarm. The future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has attempted to disarm with limited success thus far, is a matter of concern.US personnel and equipment have completed a "orderly departure" from the air base in Irbil, in the semi-autonomous Kurdish area of northern Iraq, according to a statement from Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell.He declared, "This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region." "It also signifies a change from a coalition mission during the war to an Iraqi-led security operation backed by a more regular bilateral security relationship."The US withdrawal marked the start of a "new phase, one defined by Iraq's sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends," according to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who oversaw the handover ceremony.According to him, the government would make sure that non-state organizations no longer possess weapons, and Iraqi security forces will carry on the battle against IS.In order to overthrow Saddam Hussein, American forces invaded Iraq in 2003. The US forces withdrew in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities called back a smaller US-led military mission to help combat the Islamic State group, which had seized large parts of the country during its rapid expansion.In 2024, Washington and Baghdad decided to end the campaign after the terrorist group had been reduced to dispersed sleeper cells.Last year, the majority of US outposts in Iraq were evacuated, but hundreds of troops remained in the northern Kurdish region, which is semi-autonomous.Bases there have regularly been attacked since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias have also coordinated attacks against Saudi Arabia with Yemen's Houthi rebels.Iraq government first linked up the Sept. 30 deadline for the withdrawal of US forces with the unconditional disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.While a few less influential of the militias agreed to turn in their weapons, the big groups aligned with Iran either dismissed the idea or put up conditions that the government would be unlikely to agree for the meeting.Al-Zaidi later retracted the deadline. Earlier this month, he told the New York Times that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.The impact of the United States' withdrawal may not be so apparent, and it is particularly given that the United States' military power has already been reduced. Still, officials in the Iraqi Kurdish region have expressed worries over the departure and especially over the removal of the United States' air defense systems.The Peshmerga Ministry of the Kurdish regional government said that their region has been hit by more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent US-Iran conflict."Under these complex circumstances, the departure of the Unites states from the Kurdistan Region without a provision of a defense systemis a matter of concern," the statement said.Meanwhile, Iran-allied groups in Iraq have expressed their delight at the US withdrawal."The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty," Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official of the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.He also issued a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to continue American plans and threatened that "any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means."You use AI every day.
