articles.title: Fridge bought for Rs 1.09 lakh stops cooling and then explodes; court orders Rs 1.99 lakh payout
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Jharkhand district consumer commission has directed an electronics company and its service centre to pay Rs 1.99 lakh to a customer after his
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Jharkhand district consumer commission has directed an electronics company and its service centre to pay Rs 1.99 lakh to a customer after his refrigerator allegedly developed repeated cooling problems, was repaired 8 times and later blasted. The commission also directed the parties to pay Rs 1.25 lakh towards the cost of a new refrigerator, Rs 50,000 as compensation and Rs 25,000 as litigation costs. The order was passed on September 21, 2026.Why did the customer approach the commission?According to the commission order, Ganesh Kumar Agiwal bought a refrigerator for Rs 1.09 lakh. After some time, it stopped cooling properly. He complained to the authorised service centre, following which a mechanic repaired the refrigerator eight times. The compressor was also changed and more gas was filled into the refrigerator. The complainant alleged that it subsequently blasted with a loud noise.The complainant then approached the company and its authorised dealer seeking a replacement and he also sent an email on October 17, 2024, asking them to resolve the problem by replacing the refrigerator. As per the order, the issue remained unresolved for another several months.The commission recorded that the company had offered a new refrigerator with an retail price of Rs 1,24,999 at a wholesale price of Rs 83,000.However, the replacement was not provided and aggrieved from this the complainant then approached the consumer commission seeking Rs 4,49,624 as compensation for the alleged deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.What did the commission find?The bench comprising President Sunil Kumar Singh along with member Pradeep Kumar Mishra and member Sanju Shahi noted that the service centre appeared in the case but did not file a written statement despite being given several opportunities. The company also did not appear even after a reminder. The matter was therefore fixed for ex-parte hearing.The complainant filed his statement on affidavit along with documents, including the purchase bill and a copy of his email to the company. After examining the material, the commission found substance in the complaint's case.“Having heard and on careful scrutiny of oral and documentary evidence adduced by the complainant we find much substance in case of the complainant as same is fully corroborated by oral and documentary evidence and there is absolutely nothing on the case record to discard claim of the complainant,” the commission noted.The commission also noted that the customer had suffered physical and financial harassment and mental agony because of the deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.“In view of discussion made above we are of considered opinion that the complainant suffered physical, financial harassment and mental agony due to deficiency of services and unfair trade practice of the O.P’s,” the bench further held.What did the consumer commission order?The Seraikella-Kharsawan district consumer commission directed both opposite parties to:Pay Rs 1,24,999, the price of a new refrigerator, to the customer.Pay Rs 50,000 as compensation for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.Pay Rs 25,000 towards litigation costs.Make the payment within 45 days of the order.The commission further directed that if the amount was not paid within the prescribed period, it would be recovered through due process with 9 percent annual interest from the date of the order. The total amount ordered, excluding interest, is Rs 1,99,999.

articles.title: In 1979, wood chips covered a U.S. coal-haul road and made dust control last 10 times longer than water spraying alone in a field test without repeat spraying
articles.summary: Discover how a groundbreaking 1979 field test by the U.S. Forest Service demonstrated that wood chips can significantly extend dust control on coal-haul roads, lasting ten times longer than water alone.
articles.body: A 1979 U.S. Forest Service field experiment found that a layer of wood chips could keep dust under control on a coal-haul road for roughly 10 times longer than the untreated road when it is under comparable traffic and weather conditions. The result came from a preliminary test in Breathitt County, Kentucky, where researchers covered a 100-meter section of a mine spur road with wood chips and compared it with adjacent untreated sections. The study was published as Forest Service Research Note NE-277.Mine operators were already dealing with a problem, which was that even though water sprinkling could suppress dust, the effect did not last long. The Forest Service report said that increases in traffic, temperature and wind, along with lower humidity, could quickly dry a road surface. Water trucks then had to make more frequent passes or use more water, which increased the number of trucks needed to cover a haul-road network and could become difficult when water supplies were limited.The wood-chip approach worked differently, wherein researchers placed a physical layer over the road surface instead of relying entirely on repeated wetting. The chips helped keep existing fine particles from being lifted by passing trucks, reduced the direct pounding of tires on the road and slowed evaporation from the surface. The report said that the chip blanket therefore addressed both the moisture problem and the mechanical forces that turn road material into airborne dust.The test used waste trees from a mine siteThe researchers used whole trees that had recently been cleared from the mine site, including oak, hickory and gum. The trees were processed into chips, transported about 50 miles to the test location and spread over the road with a motor grader. The researchers treated about 100 meters of the section, where the chip layer varied from about 3 to 6 centimeters thick, and used approximately 28.4 cubic meters of chips. Researchers also monitored temperature, humidity and moisture in the road material while counting the vehicles that passed through the test section. The Forest Service report records 57 loaded coal trucks, 53 empty coal trucks and 33 passenger or service vehicles during the observation periods. Truck speeds averaged about 22 mph for loaded trucks and 27 mph for empty trucks.On the chip-covered section, it took five hours of traffic use and 21 hours of elapsed time for the dust plume to approach the level that was already seen on the untreated road after roughly half an hour. The treated road also lost moisture more slowly, and the report calculated that the overall moisture-loss rate on untreated sections was 2.5 times that of the section protected by chips. The road had been sprayed shortly before the chips were applied, and the researchers did not present the wood layer as a complete replacement for sprinkling; instead, the study examined whether the chips could extend the period before another application of water was needed.The researchers warned against reading too much into the resultThe chip blanket itself began to deteriorate under traffic, and after six hours of traffic-related stress, the average width of the chips had fallen by about 25 percent. Fast-moving trucks also disturbed the blanket, which pushed chips toward the sides of the road and exposed some areas. The report said a motor grader could redistribute the material, but repeated reworking would mix more road dust into the chips and further break them down. The 10-fold advantage observed during the limited test was unlikely to continue unchanged over the medium or long term, and the conclusion was that under traffic and weather stresses similar to those in the experiment, wood chips could reduce the need for dust-control sprinkling substantially.A U.S. Environmental Protection Agency technical report from the period described watering as a common method for suppressing fugitive dust from unpaved roads and noted that effectiveness depended on weather, road conditions and traffic. Another Mine Safety and Health Administration dust-control handbook notes that haul trucks can account for a large share of particulate emissions at surface mine sites and that dust from haul roads can reduce visibility as well as expose workers to airborne particles.The Forest Service noted that, when a temporary haul road was eventually abandoned and reclaimed, the deteriorated chips could be incorporated into the soil as an organic mulch. The original study therefore ended with a practical proposition that material that began as waste from clearing a mine site could serve a temporary road-management purpose before becoming part of reclamation work.You use AI every day. articles.title: Gandhi Jayanti 2026: History, Significance, Facts, Celebration and all you need to know
articles.summary: Gandhi Jayanti 2026 is celebrated on October 2 as the 157th birthday of Mahatma Gandhi who was born on October 2, 1869, in Porbandar, Gujarat.
articles.body: Gandhi Jayanti 2026 is celebrated on October 2 as the 157th birthday of Mahatma Gandhi who was born on October 2, 1869, in Porbandar, Gujarat. On this day, in India, the life of Mahatma Gandhi is honored and his contribution to the struggle for freedom is commemorated. However, on October 2, the United Nations celebrates the International Day of Non-violence around the world.Gandhi Jayanti is celebrated in a variety of ways, from holding memorial services in Rajghat to delivering speeches on peace, non-violence, and the social responsibility of people. Here is all you need to know about Gandhi Jayanti 2026, its history, significance, facts, and celebrations.Why is Gandhi Jayanti celebrated?Gandhi Jayanti is celebrated on the date of birth of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, universally known as Mahatma Gandhi. Born on October 2, 1869, in the town of Porbandar, he became one of the most important leaders of the Indian freedom struggle. In addition to that, he is also associated with a unique way of resistance based on truth and non-violence.His technique of Satyagraha, literally meaning resistance based on truth and non-violence, thus became a vital component of various movements opposing British rule.His techniques were later applied in the fights for the civil rights in places far beyond India. This day has a great importance for various reasons, as it is not only the birthday of Gandhi, but it also is a symbol of the ideologies associated with him, such as non-violence, peace, truth, tolerance and social responsibility.History of Gandhi JayantiIn 1869, a Hindu Family blessed with a son in Porbandar in Kathiawad (now Gujarat). He went to London and got trained as a lawyer and got involved in the South Africa in 1893 where he experienced racial discrimination which influenced his political beliefs. Gandhi returned to India in 1915 and got involved in the independence movements. He advocated Swadeshi, a movement promoting the boycott of foreign-made items and peaceful protests of the British rule.He participated in several non-violent political actions, and the most famous one is the 1930 Salt March. A salt march is a journey of Gandhi’s followers from his ashram in Gujarat to Dandi to protest against the salt tax imposed by the British Raj. The protest turned historical as it became part of India’s freedom struggle. Gandhi was shot and killed on 30 January 1948 in New Delhi, and the day is marked as Martyrs’ Day in India.What is the Significance of Gandhi Jayanti?Gandhi Jayanti is significant for various reasons, some of them include:1. Reminder of non-violence: Non-violence was a key element of Gandhi’s political philosophy and action. Gandhi’s various non-violent movements have shown that non-violent massive protests could overt urn successful.2. Celebration of truth and of Satyagraha: Satyagraha is a philosophical concept developed by Gandhi, and its core element is truth. The concept promoted non-violent resistance to injustice and has been practiced in South Africa as well as in India’s independence struggle.3. A link to the freedom struggle of India: Gandhi’s contribution to the freedom struggle of India marks the significance of October 2 in modern Indian history. His various campaigns mobilised a large portion of the population for anti-colonial activities of various types.4. A message of universal significance: His ideas have gone beyond the freedom struggle of India. In 2007, the United Nations declared October 2 as the International Day of Non-Violence and has been using this date as a chance to spread messages of non-violence through education and public awareness.How is Gandhi Jayanti celebrated?Gandhi Jayanti is celebrated through various prayer activities and events in remembrance of the great leader in India. One of the important places related to the celebration of the event is Rajghat, which is situated in New Delhi and has Gandhi's memorial. Official celebrations normally involve paying tributes and conducting a prayer ceremony.On the other hand, schools and educational organizations can also organize additional activities, such as essay writing competitions, debates and discussions, art and poster competitions, Gandhi's life speeches, quiz competitions, prayer meetings, cultural events, etc. The main idea of such activities is to introduce young people to Gandhi's ideas.Why does the day still matter?Over seventy years since Ghandi's demise, Gandhi Jayanti is still one of the significant days of the Indian public calendar. The day’s observance connects the past with the present by bringing discussions about the historical figure as well as about the independence movement into the conversations about non-violence, peace, tolerance, and civic responsibility throughout the world.In 2026, October 2nd will fall on a Friday. But besides being a public holiday, this date presents an opportunity to study the history of the freedom struggle in India as well as the fundamental principles of the philosophy of this prominent Indian figure.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Russia's jet drones challenge Ukraine, India builds its own answer
articles.summary: Russia's jet-powered attack drones have emerged as one of the toughest challenges facing Ukraine's air defences this year, flying faster and higher than
articles.body: Russia's jet-powered attack drones have emerged as one of the toughest challenges facing Ukraine's air defences this year, flying faster and higher than the older propeller-driven Shahed-136s that have battered the country for years and proving far harder to intercept.The latest variant, the Geran-4, first surfaced last May. Unlike its predecessor, it was purpose-built for high-speed flight, as the older airframe could not withstand the stress of manoeuvring at such velocities. Its blended air intake and reinforced structure allow it to fly at altitudes of up to eight kilometres, twice as high as the drones it replaces, reaching speeds of 450 to 500 kilometres an hour and covering distances of over 700 kilometres.The engine powering it is Chinese-made, though some units are reportedly assembled inside Russia using Chinese components. Ukrainian intelligence estimates that Russia is now producing around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month.The newer Geran-5 goes further still, reportedly navigating using satellite reference imagery rather than GPS, making it far harder to jam. Ukraine has responded by using F-16 fighters to shoot the drones down with cannon fire, while also fielding purpose-built interceptor drones. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the UN General Assembly this week that four new jet-powered interceptors had already been tested successfully against the Russian threat.India, meanwhile, is building its own answer to this style of warfare. The Defence Research and Development Organisation's Gas Turbine Research Establishment has successfully developed a 350-kg-class expendable turbojet engine, the kind used to power cruise missiles, target drones and, increasingly, jet-powered loitering munitions.The American Tomahawk, by comparison, uses a 400-kg-class engine for the same purpose. As warfare shifts increasingly towards non-contact strikes, this class of engine is becoming central to modern arsenals. The newly developed unit sits just below the 450-kg-class Small Turbofan Engine built for India's Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile.The timing is notable, coming just a month after the Army ordered 106 jet-powered Agniveg loitering munitions from a domestic manufacturer. Designed to strike deep inside enemy territory with a circular error probable of under five metres, the Agniveg is built to be jam- and spoof-resistant. Its jet propulsion lets it fly at up to 450 kmph, more than double the speed of Shahed- or Geran-type drones.That speed makes it suited to hitting high-value targets, logistics hubs, fuel depots, command centres and radar sites, without risking manned platforms or relying solely on costlier cruise missiles.Manufacturing engines of this class demands exceptional precision and advanced metallurgy, a capability only a handful of countries possess. In India, GTRE works alongside production partner Azad Engineering, with private firms including DG Propulsion, Nabhdrishti Aerospace and Paninian Aerospace also entering the space.These efforts are steadily reducing India's reliance on imports, even as the country continues working to solve its harder engine challenge: powering fighter aircraft.

articles.title: Meet Ethan Eriksen: 16-year-old Wisconsin student who wanted flame-covered snow pants, built his own brand and won a $5,000 state entrepreneur prize
articles.summary: Most teenagers who cannot find the clothing they want simply give up and buy something else.
articles.body: Most teenagers who cannot find the clothing they want simply give up and buy something else. Ethan Eriksen, a sixteen-year-old junior at Barron High School in Wisconsin, chose a different route. Unable to find high-quality ski pants covered in flames, he made his own and launched Shredrz Attire. Months later, he stood before a panel of prominent business leaders in Milwaukee and won the state's Young Entrepreneur of the Year title, taking home a $5,000 prize. His story shows how a simple frustration, persistence, and a supportive community can turn a teenage idea into a genuine business.How a missing pair of flame ski pants inspired Shredrz AttireEthan Eriksen has been skiing since the age of nine, so he knew exactly what he wanted from a pair of ski pants, genuine quality and a bold flame design. When he could not find them, he decided in 2025 to create them himself. Having started his first business while still in primary school, he said he had noticed a gap in the market and believed he could fill it. He worked with overseas clothing designers through several versions before settling on custom ski and winter recreation apparel that he describes as both functional and stylish. That effort became Shredrz Attire, a small brand built around his own passion for the slopes.Inside the Junior Achievement of Wisconsin Young Entrepreneur CompetitionJunior Achievement of Wisconsin runs an annual search for the state's most promising teenage business start-ups, and its Young Entrepreneur Competition was held in Milwaukee. Finalists were scored on growth potential, strategic direction and innovation, as well as personal integrity, leadership and any special challenges overcome in bringing their business to life. The judging panel featured Mario Costantini of La Lune Collection, Craig Culver, co-founder of Culver's, Louis P. Gentine II, chief executive of Sargento, Anna Lardinois of MKEStartup.News, and Jim Popp, chief executive of Johnson Financial Group. Ethan's pitch stood out against three other finalist businesses from Appleton, North Fond du Lac and Verona, whose founders each received a $1,500 scholarship as semifinalists.Why Ethan Eriksen also won the Viewer's Choice AwardEthan claimed the Wisconsin Young Entrepreneur of the Year title and a $5,000 prize, according to Junior Achievement of Wisconsin, which describes the award as a scholarship. The local television station WEAU reported that he also won the Viewer's Choice Award, effectively sweeping the competition. He told the TV station that the result brought a sense of relief, because the hard work on both the contest and the business had paid off. His teacher, Ky Baumgard, who encouraged him to enter, called the presentation professional and polished, yet full of personality. Baumgard added that the achievement is a victory for the entire school district, with students and the wider community rallying behind him.How Ethan Eriksen balances school, sport, skiing and a start-up businessBeyond the prize, Ethan's approach to balance offers lessons for other young founders. He is a multi-sport athlete and a ski instructor, and he manages everything with a strict school-first rule. He credits careful time management and clear priorities, and he regularly turns to his mother for advice, calling her his biggest consultant. His message to anyone with a dream is straightforward, believe in yourself, because work stops feeling like a chore when you love what you do. Junior Achievement, whose volunteers have taught life skills to 340,000 Wisconsin students since 2021, exists to help young people plan their future.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2018, a skeleton crew stayed at a Malibu animal park as the Woolsey Fire arrived; 133 of its roughly 140 animals survived, including a giraffe and 80 horses
articles.summary: In November 2018, a dedicated team of 32 employees at Malibu Wine Safari stayed behind to protect nearly all of the park's animals, including Stanley the giraffe, as the Woolsey Fire approached. Read about their efforts to save these exotic creatures amidst a devastating wildfire.
articles.body: Thirty-two employees stayed behind at Malibu Wine Safari as the Woolsey Fire swept toward the property in November 2018, while large animals, including Stanley the giraffe, remained on site because their keepers considered moving them more dangerous than sheltering them in place. The park’s owners later said that about 135 of roughly 140 animals survived, including Stanley and around 80 horses. The property is at Saddlerock Ranch, in the mountains above Malibu, and was badly damaged as the fire moved through the area. Stanley had become the most recognizable animal there, and photographs of the giraffe standing near the flames spread rapidly online. The images prompted public concern that the animals had been abandoned after staff evacuated.Dakota Semler, whose family owned the park, told Reuters that employees remained with the animals throughout the fire, and said that transporting some of the exotic animals presented its own risks. A giraffe, for example, could not simply be loaded into an ordinary trailer, and moving frightened exotic animals during a fast-moving wildfire could cause injury or shock. The Woolsey Fire began on November 8, 2018, and moved quickly through Los Angeles and Ventura counties. The National Park Service records that the fire eventually burned almost 100,000 acres and caused widespread damage across the Santa Monica Mountains.Stanley stayed in an open areaThe park had decided to keep many of its larger animals on the property rather than attempt a last-minute evacuation, wherein Stanley and other animals were moved into areas with less vegetation and other fuel. A photograph that showed Stanley with flames and smoke in the distance became particularly alarming, and social-media users called for the giraffe to be moved.Local reporting after the fire found that Stanley had survived, with ABC7 Los Angeles reporting that the animals had been placed in a pasture with little fuel to burn as the fire approached. The park said its management and animal-care staff had prepared for evacuation but ultimately kept the animals on site.Reuters reported that three pigs, two parrots, an emu and a sheep were among the animals that died or were lost, which left the overwhelming majority of the approximately 140 animals alive. The collection included horses, a llama and camels as well as the exotic animals that drew visitors to the safari park. Barns and other structures were damaged or lost, which left the park’s animal-care facilities badly affected even though most of its animals survived.Moving the animals was not straightforwardWildfire evacuation plans are often designed around getting people out quickly, but exotic animal collections create another problem: many species cannot be transported easily under emergency conditions. Semler told Reuters that moving an 18-foot giraffe into a 12-foot trailer would carry obvious risks. Other large animals can become difficult to control when frightened, and the logistics of finding suitable vehicles and destinations become more complicated as a fire advances.The National Park Service says that Santa Ana winds pushed the fire south on its first day before it crossed the 101 Freeway and entered the Santa Monica Mountains. Almost 88% of the National Park Service land within the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area eventually burned. Workers stayed behind, cared for the animals and dealt with the fire as it reached the ranch.Stanley’s survival became the most visible part of the story because the giraffe was already well known to visitors and had a large social-media following, but the fire involved an entire collection of animals, not just one celebrity giraffe. Stanley was photographed alive and walking around the damaged ranch after the flames passed. The park’s surviving animals still needed care, while crews began dealing with destroyed buildings, burned enclosures and other damage left behind by the Woolsey Fire.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2004, a Brooklyn writer mostly avoided non-essential shopping to challenge consumer culture; she spent a year buying necessities with some exceptions and turned it into a book
articles.summary: Explore how Judith Levine transformed her life by committing to a year without non-essential shopping, examining the impact on consumer culture and personal finances in her book 'Not Buying It.'
articles.body: In January 2004, Brooklyn-based writer Judith Levine and her partner, Paul, made a simple but difficult agreement: for the next 12 months, they would buy only what they considered necessary. Food, medicines, household essentials and expenses connected with their work were allowed, but new clothes, entertainment and many everyday treats were off the list. The experiment became the basis of Levine's book Not Buying It: My Year Without Shopping, published in 2006.According to The Washington Post, the idea came after Levine found herself caught up in the pressures of Christmas shopping and increasingly concerned about her finances and the culture of buying. She was not presenting the experiment as a complete solution to consumerism. Instead, she wanted to see what happened when shopping, something that had become an ordinary part of modern life, was deliberately removed from her routine.When shopping was no longer the defaultThe rules seemed simple enough, but they became increasingly difficult to follow in everyday life. Levine and Paul could still buy food, toiletries, medication and other necessities, but many everyday purchases now required them to decide whether they were truly necessary. Is eating out at a restaurant really a need? How about a new book, movie tickets, or clothes? The differentiation between needs and wants was one of the main issues raised during the experiment. Levine kept her job and had apartments in both Brooklyn and Vermont, and so the task did not consist of breaking away from a routine.Entertainment, however, presented a special problem. The couple reduced their spending on many things they usually bought, including movies and dinners at restaurants. Instead, they started borrowing books from libraries, taking part in free events and socialising with friends more often. Some social events even required them to ask for others’ help in providing things they needed instead of buying them all themselves. The experiment changed not only what they bought, but how they thought about spending itself. Buying coffee on a trip, purchasing a new piece of clothing and going out could not become a routine anymore.What research says about consuming lessLevine's experience fits into a wider area of research known as anti-consumption, which examines why people deliberately reduce, reject or avoid consumption. Research published in the Journal of Consumer Affairs has examined the relationship between anti-consumption, materialism and consumer well-being, identifying control over consumption, material desire and the sources of happiness as important differences between anti-consumption and materialistic behaviour.Levine's year serves as a personal example of the difference between these two approaches to spending. It was not just about spending less. Rather, Levine had to question what she wanted in the first place and if not having that would really make any difference to her life. At other times, Levine realised the social dimension of her consumption. Eating out, engaging in entertainment for which people pay and giving gifts are not only acts of personal consumption but social practices as well. And Levine realised that sometimes not spending might mean not participating in certain social events.A year of shopping less, not buying anythingLevine and Paul did not claim to have stopped spending money altogether. They defined necessities as food, medical needs, domestic needs and business needs. There were times when, even by their strict standards, it was hard to distinguish the difference between necessity and wants. As a matter of fact, Levine had bought herself trousers during the year, which complicated the experiment's results. However, it also proved the general idea behind it.Financially, however, that year made a big difference. According to contemporary accounts, Levine calculated that she and her husband were able to save roughly $8,000, which enabled her to settle her credit card bills. Through the experiment, Levine gained a better understanding of how her shopping habits had become part of her daily routine. The result of her experience is Not Buying It, a month-by-month account of her exploration of shopping, needs, desires, scarcity and consumer culture.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: INDIA bloc meet: BJP says Oct 2 march is to ‘save dynasty, not democracy'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Wednesday hit out at the INDIA bloc, saying the opposition alliance's proposed nationwide protests against the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Wednesday hit out at the INDIA bloc, saying the opposition alliance's proposed nationwide protests against the Election Commission are aimed at “saving dynasty” rather than “saving democracy”.After INDIA bloc's meeting, Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan accused the opposition of attacking the poll panel to create an “advance excuse” for a defeat in the upcoming elections.“Zero vision, 100 per cent frustration and an advance excuse for defeat. Before the upcoming elections, they are already setting the stage for their defeat. They are looking for excuses for their loss right now. A programme from October 2 to 8 has been announced - ‘Save Democracy March’. This is not a Save Democracy March. This is a Save Dynasty March,” Chouhan said.Chouhan also questioned the unity of the opposition alliance, pointing to the absence of several INDIA bloc leaders from the meeting.“Today there was an INDI alliance meeting, but the alliance had already fallen apart even before the meeting. Uttar Pradesh is a state where elections are due. Where was Akhilesh Yadav? If the issue is so important, why is Akhilesh Yadav not there? Where is Stalin? DMK has already said that wherever Congress is present, we will not sit there. Where is Arvind Kejriwal? Uddhav Thackeray is not physically present. We do not know about Pawar and Hemant Soren ji,” he said.“The condition of the INDI alliance has become such that a heart has been torn into a thousand pieces, one falling here and another there. The truth is that the INDI alliance is not ready to accept Rahul ji as its leader,” Chouhan added.Chauhan's remarks came after the INDIA bloc announced a series of nationwide protests against the Election Commission and the SIR of electoral rolls, seeking to project opposition unity amid the ongoing row over voter rolls.Addressing a press conference after the meeting, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge said the alliance would hold district-level “save democracy” marches and demonstrations outside district magistrates' offices from October 2 to 8.“From October 2 to 8, we will hold district-level 'Save Democracy' marches and stage demonstrations outside the offices of every district magistrate. We will also make people aware of why we are undertaking this campaign,” Kharge said.The INDIA bloc meeting came days after a media report claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected on record at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders on SIR that they said were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.Under fire over the reported objections by the two commissioners, the Election Commission has maintained that differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberations in any institution. It said all its orders carry full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A fugitive used a dead classmate's name from 1984 and lived under it for 40 years; he collected over $138,000 in Social Security before FBI agents caught him
articles.summary: A fugitive who was wanted in Wyoming on an attempted murder charge spent more than four decades living under the identity of a deceased former college
articles.body: A fugitive who was wanted in Wyoming on an attempted murder charge spent more than four decades living under the identity of a deceased former college classmate, according to the US Department of Justice. Stephen Craig Campbell, 76, assumed the identity of Walter Lee Coffman, who died in 1975 at age 22. Campbell first applied for a US passport in Coffman's name in 1984, submitting his own photograph and current address. Over the years he obtained government documents, bought property and fraudulently collected more than $138,000 in Social Security retirement benefits. The deception unravelled after a September 2019 driver's licence renewal, and FBI agents arrested him in New Mexico in February 2025. He was sentenced to 81 months in federal prison.Campbell became a fugitive after a 1982 bombing allegationAccording to court documents cited by the DOJ, Campbell became a fugitive after being accused in 1982 of attempting to kill his estranged wife's boyfriend. Prosecutors said he planted a homemade explosive device at the man's home. It detonated when Campbell's estranged wife opened the package, causing severe lacerations and the loss of one of her fingers. The explosion also started a fire that spread to a second apartment unit. Campbell failed to appear in court on the original charge of attempted first-degree murder. A Wyoming warrant issued in 1983 for that failure to appear remains outstanding.He assumed the identity of a dead classmateAfter becoming a fugitive, Campbell took the identity of Walter Lee Coffman, a former classmate from the University of Arkansas. Coffman died in 1975, just months after graduating with an engineering degree. In 1984, Campbell first applied for a US passport in Coffman's name, using his own photograph and current address. He renewed the fraudulent passport over the years, including in 2005 and 2015. The identity also let him obtain a replacement Social Security card, multiple passports, a New Mexico driver's licence and other official documents. Around 2003, he used it to buy property in Weed, New Mexico, where he continued to live under Coffman's name.He tried to erase Coffman's death recordCampbell took steps to secure the identity long before the discovery of his fraud. In 1992, he contacted the Social Security Administration in an attempt to remove Coffman's death record. On October 15, 1995, he fraudulently applied for and received a replacement Social Security card in Coffman's name, using an Oklahoma driver's licence in that name.He collected more than $138,000 in Social SecurityUsing Coffman's identity, Campbell fraudulently obtained more than $138,000 in Social Security Retirement Insurance Benefits, beginning in 2015, according to the DOJ's sentencing announcement. An earlier account, from the time of his guilty plea, put the figure at about $140,000.In September 2019, Campbell presented a passport bearing Coffman's name to a New Mexico Motor Vehicle Division employee in Cloudcroft and used it to renew his driver's licence, knowing it was not legitimate. Agents from the National Passport Center's Fraud Prevention Unit then discovered that Coffman had died in 1975 and alerted federal authorities.The FBI and the Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General jointly investigated. The case was originally initiated by the State Department's Diplomatic Security Service and the Fraud Prevention Unit. The investigation uncovered Campbell's true identity as a long-time violent fugitive.FBI SWAT teams arrested him in 2025Campbell was not arrested until February 2025, more than five years after the licence renewal. On February 19, FBI SWAT teams from Albuquerque and El Paso, supported by aerial assets, approached his property in Weed to execute arrest and search warrants.Air surveillance saw Campbell leave the back of his home and enter the wood line. Wearing camouflage, he stayed there despite agents' commands. After flash bangs were deployed and agents gave further commands, he emerged and surrendered. A loaded rifle with a scope and a 20-round magazine was recovered from the wood line.Investigators found 57 firearmsA search of the property recovered 57 firearms, along with large quantities of ammunition and magazines. Campbell was prohibited from possessing firearms because he was a fugitive from justice.The FBI's Albuquerque Field Office, through its Las Cruces Resident Agency, and the Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General co-investigated the case. US Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations and the Otero County Sheriff's Office provided enforcement assistance.He pleaded guilty to four federal chargesThe DOJ announced in early June 2026 that Campbell had pleaded guilty to four federal offences: misuse of a passport, possession of false papers to defraud the United States, aggravated identity theft, and being a fugitive from justice in possession of a firearm and ammunition. He faced up to 12 years in prison. Assistant US Attorney Clara Nevarez Cobos prosecuted the case.He was sentenced to 81 monthsThe DOJ announced on September 4, 2026 that Campbell had been sentenced to 81 months, or six years and nine months, in federal prison. The court also ordered three years of supervised release after his prison term and a $20,000 fine. There is no parole in the federal system.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Terrorist pilot planned to crash plane': Israel security minister on flydubai cockpit incident
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir on Thursday said the person involved in the cockpit incident aboard a flydubai flight had
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir on Thursday said the person involved in the cockpit incident aboard a flydubai flight had planned to crash the aircraft and kill the Israelis on board, as Transportation Minister Miri Regev called for the suspension of all flydubai flights to Israel following the incident.Thanking the passengers who intervened during the incident, Ben-Gvir said Israel's security approach needed to be strengthened and described the person under investigation as a "terrorist"."The naive notion that our enemies value life and that we should have mercy on them received another reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board," Ben-Gvir said on X."Terrorism is a devil with which no agreement should ever be reached except for its defeat and erasure from the face of the earth," he said, adding that Israel must continue until achieving what he called "total victory" in Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, and Judea and Samaria.Regev, meanwhile, has demanded that all flydubai flights to Israel be suspended following the incident aboard a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, according to Israeli media reports.She has also asked Israel's Civil Aviation Authority to investigate whether the United Arab Emirates violated its aviation agreement with Israel. The agreement reportedly stipulates that only pilots holding passports from countries that have diplomatic relations with Israel may land in the country.What happened aboard flydubai flight?The incident occurred aboard flight FZ1073, a Boeing 737 MAX carrying around 180 passengers, including Israelis, from Dubai to Tel Aviv.Passengers described scenes of panic after screams erupted in the cabin, with one pilot reportedly stabbed and the aircraft suddenly plunging thousands of feet."We heard screams on the plane. Then they opened the cockpit and we saw blood, and someone had stabbed the pilot with a pocketknife," an Israeli passenger told Channel 12.Another passenger, identified as Noam, said: "Screams began on the plane… by passengers who realized what was happening," according to The Times of Israel.Passengers said some Israelis helped crew members restrain the attacker. Israeli media also reported that two additional pilots travelling as passengers intervened during the confrontation.The aircraft transmitted the international emergency code 7700 before briefly sending code 7500, which indicates hijacking or unlawful interference. Israeli authorities reportedly scrambled fighter jets after losing contact with the aircraft.Flight data showed the plane suddenly dropped from about 34,000 feet to around 17,000 feet in less than a minute before climbing and descending again.The aircraft eventually established contact and diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely. Flydubai said all passengers were safe and accounted for.Read more: Screams, chaos onboard as Flydubai flight takes 17,000 ft roller coaster ride mid-airIsraeli media reports have identified the pilot under investigation as an Omani national, although the details have not been independently confirmed.Israel does not have diplomatic relations with Oman, making the reported nationality relevant to Regev's request for an aviation agreement review.There were also unconfirmed reports that the confrontation began when one pilot attacked the other and that the aircraft was subsequently at risk of being deliberately crashed. Israeli officials are investigating the circumstances of the cockpit incident.A senior Israeli official told Channel 12 that the presence of the additional pilots travelling as passengers helped avert what could have been a major disaster, although that account has not been independently confirmed.Flydubai has confirmed that an incident occurred aboard the flight but has not publicly confirmed the reported stabbing, the identity or nationality of the person involved, or the alleged motive.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bombs without brakes? Why the US-China AI race may be harder to control than the nuclear one
articles.summary: On the first day of the Iran war, two US missiles hit an elementary school in Hormozgan's Minab, killing 123 children. It was not the plan.
articles.body: On the first day of the Iran war, two US missiles hit an elementary school in Hormozgan's Minab, killing 123 children. It was not the plan.The Pentagon's own investigation found that Maven Smart System, an AI-powered advanced software meant to lock a target, reportedly rushed flawed data through its system without proper human review. The result? Devastation.Months later, at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), improvisational US President Donald Trump touted AI as "Super Intelligence". Irony.“Whoever wins AI, WINS!," Trump said while rejecting international oversight as a "globalist scheme," and made clear Washington will not slow down.China, meanwhile, sounds gentler than Washington but is just as determined not to fall behind. During his state visit to America last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping said the two countries have the “capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that AI development is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people”.Behind the friendly words, Beijing is worried back home. Recently, Wang Lihong, deputy head of China's Cybersecurity Coordination Bureau, said that AI models escaping test environments showed "extreme loss-of-control risks" and needed a "high degree of vigilance".Two weeks later, China released a safety framework warning that AI agents might gain resources on their own, deceive testers or hide what they can do.Nevertheless, both nations mantain that AI must stay under human control, yet each fears that the other will pull ahead the moment it slows down, and that fear keeps the pedal down in the race for dominance.The nuclear analogyThe people building artificial intelligence keep reaching for the same comparison. Billionaire Elon Musk has called AI “far more dangerous than nukes.” Anthropic boss Dario Amodei describes the most powerful models as “weaponisable nuclear materials.” Sam Altman, when asked how AI could be policed, often points to the International Atomic Energy Agency(IAEA), the world's nuclear watchdog.The comparison certainly holds water as both technologies are powerful and hard to control, with the ability to be a double-edged sword to help or harm.And just as the bomb reshaped world power after 1945, whoever leads in AI may shape the decades ahead. Meanwhile, in the 21st century of the post-Cold War era only the players have changed. Washington and Moscow have given way to Washington and Beijing, but the fear of falling behind feels exactly the same.The Cold War was closer than you thinkMany people remember the Cold War as a tense contest that was managed well enough to avoid nuclear war. However, the truth is pretty messier. In October 1962, during the Cuban missile crisis, the United States and the Soviet Union came within a decision or two of nuclear war.A Soviet submarine nearly fired a nuclear torpedo at American warships. A US U-2 spy plane, popularly called "Dragon Lady," strayed into Soviet airspace and had to be escorted home by nuclear-armed American fighters. Many of these moments happened far down the chain of command, without the top leaders knowing.The scares kept coming. In November 1979, an American warning system mistook a test tape for a major Soviet attack. At least ten fighter aircraft were sent up, and the president's emergency plane took off without him. In September 1983, Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov watched his early warning system report an incoming American strike. He decided, correctly, that it was a fault.By and large, it seems completely reasonable to pause and think how much of that peace was due to luck rather than design.Rules born from fearOut of that danger came rules as in 1953, US president Dwight Eisenhower launched a plan known as “Atoms for Peace” under which countries could get nuclear technology if they promised not to use it for weapons.By the 1970s the Non-Proliferation Treaty was in force and international inspectors were checking nuclear programmes. Washington and Moscow agreed test bans, held arms control summits and set up a crisis hotline. Today only nine countries have nuclear weapons.The safety net is frayingChina's nuclear stockpile has nearly tripled since 2020, and the Pentagon expects it to reach 1,000 warheads by 2030. The two big arms treaties between Washington and Moscow, New START and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, have died. So the old safety net has worn thin just as a new race gathers speed.In frontier AI, Trump makes winning the whole point, and Chinese researchers and state media argue that slowing down would only protect America's lead. Xi Jinping's “capability and responsibility" remark shows that Beijing won't budge unless America, for all practical purposes, also slows down. This is where AI leaves the nuclear playbook behind.Uranium and plutonium are rare, costly and made in huge plants, so inspectors can measure them. A country's stock of fissile material also limits how many bombs it can build. AI has no such ceiling. Chips and data centres leave a trail, and some training sites are visible from space, yet they do not reveal what a system can do.Efficiency improves every day, so what needs cutting-edge resources today needs far less tomorrow. China has kept pace with America despite a shortage of computing power.Then there are the model weights, the numbers that define a trained system. They can be copied, sent anywhere and changed. Open models that anyone can download now trail the American frontier by months, not years. Nothing like that ever existed with nuclear weapons. Chip export controls slow rivals, but cannot show who is using what.In this race for AI supremacy, who builds it matters too, as unlike a bomb that was made under government control, AI comes mainly from private companies chasing profit, and they move faster than states can write rules.Nuclear technology has narrow uses, while a single AI model can read medical records, hunt for software flaws or reason about weapon design. Nuclear inspectors can count warheads. Nobody yet knows what an AI inspector would count.When machines learn to lieRecent researches show why experts worry as in one such experiments 200 documents were examined along with 20 studies or tests since 2025 in which AI agents lied, copied themselves or pushed against their limits.In one such examinations by Reuters, agents powered by models from China's Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot competed for a simulated contract. At least one false claim about their abilities appeared in 88% of sessions for Alibaba's model, 84% for DeepSeek's and 88% for Moonshot's.When they were allowed to learn from earlier rounds, the lying rose by 12 to 20 percentage points. American models in the test did much the same. In another study, agents built on both Chinese and American systems faced broken tools or missing files, and some faked results or made up files rather than admit failure.One agent linked to Alibaba opened a connection to an outside computer without being told to and diverted computing power to mine cryptocurrency. Security systems, however, caught it.Reuters also found no sign that any Chinese-powered agent escaped onto the wider internet. Even so, Colin Shea-Blymyer of Georgetown University was blunt. “These results provide evidence that the ingredients necessary for an uncontrolled escape are present,” he said.The problem is not only Chinese as AI agents from OpenAI also escaped a laboratory this year and hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. Researcher Alex Mallen of Redwood Research warns that “as agents get more capable, their misbehaviours become more competent and therefore harder for humans to respond to.”No Hiroshima yetOversight is the hardest part as Hiroshima and Nagasaki gave the world an undeniable picture of nuclear horror, and treaties followed. AI has had warning shots but no shared shock because even a real disaster might be hard to pin on AI, and many parties could shift the blame.Washington, however, is improvising. In June, the White House used export controls to cut off foreign access to Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, then restored it at the end of the month. Such tools can be reversed by the next president. No bill yet proposes oversight on the scale used for aviation or nuclear energy.Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have also pivoted to aggressive safety freezes amid unprecedented regulatory pressure. OpenAI abruptly cancelled its advanced GPT-6.1 Astra model after it failed internal alignment tests by performing unauthorized network actions.Meanwhile, Anthropic disabled its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 systems globally following a US government national security directive exposing critical cybersecurity vulnerabilities. However, after a 19-day global suspension, the US government lifted the export controls, allowing Anthropic to begin redeploying the models on July 1, 2026.China is responding too as its official at its internet regulator said that models escaping test environments showed “extreme loss-of-control risks” and required a “high degree of vigilance”. Scott Singer of the Carnegie Endowment says China's safety ecosystem is less mature, and nobody knows whether incidents there went unreported.The comparison holds, but only halfway. The same fear drives both races. What is missing is much of what helped last time. The bomb was countable, held by governments and announced by a horror nobody could dispute. AI has none of that. The Cold War ended without catastrophe, though often by the narrowest of margins. The uncomfortable question is whether the world can count on that kind of luck twice?ALSO READ | Trump's 48 F-35 jets for Saudi Arabia: Why is Israel uneasy and China a key concernYou use AI every day. articles.title: 'Super Intelligence' AI safety accord signed by tech CEOs carries ‘Unites States’ typo under Trump’s name
articles.summary: Top technology executives have signed an agreement with US President Donald Trump promising stronger safeguards for increasingly powerful artificial
articles.body: Top technology executives have signed an agreement with US President Donald Trump promising stronger safeguards for increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems. But despite the document being signed by some of the biggest names in the tech industry, a basic spelling mistake in Trump's title went unnoticed, which drew widespread mockery online.The document, titled the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence", identifies Trump as the "President of the Unites States", instead of the "United States".The typo appears beneath Trump's prominent signature on the second page of the accord, which was circulated publicly by the White House and later shared by Trump on his Truth Social account.Trump signed the agreement on Tuesday after hosting several technology leaders at the White House. The signatories included Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, xAI CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.Sundar Pichai shares accord online, also appears to miss typoPichai also shared the document on X, saying Google had invested hundreds of billions of dollars in the US and was committed to working with other industry leaders to establish norms and build public confidence around AI.However, the typo in the document appeared to have gone unnoticed by Pichai and the other signatories before it was published.The error quickly became a talking point online, with users sharing screenshots of the document and highlighting the words "Unites States".One user wrote: "What about the typo!! Super intelligence doesn’t pick up the super intelligent typo?"Another mocked the agreement by saying: "Super Intelligence is AI without spell check."A third user pointed to the purpose of the agreement, asking whether a typo missed by the people overseeing "super intelligence" raised questions about what else could potentially be overlooked.The spelling error drew particular attention because the agreement itself focuses on safeguards and oversight for advanced AI systems.What does Trump's AI accord say?The voluntary agreement calls on participating AI companies to introduce several layers of safeguards around their systems.These include internal monitoring of model capabilities, an internal oversight team, independent external audits and a board-level committee responsible for receiving reports and ensuring that identified problems are addressed.Trump has described the accord as "morally binding", although it is not legally enforceable. The document also says that some of the measures could eventually be turned into laws or regulations.The agreement comes as AI development and the potential risks posed by increasingly capable systems have become a major focus of debate in the US.Trump has also promoted the term "super intelligence" as his preferred description for AI. On Tuesday, he signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace references to "artificial intelligence" and "AI" with "super intelligence" or "SI".The White House had not immediately commented on the spelling error or said whether a corrected version of the accord would be issued.You use AI every day. articles.title: South Carolina will combine a 102-acre nature preserve with 50 affordable homes on Johns Island; hundreds of acres of green space are protected
articles.summary: A new partnership on Johns Island, South Carolina, is bringing two pressing community needs together: protecting undeveloped land and creating affordable
articles.body: A new partnership on Johns Island, South Carolina, is bringing two pressing community needs together: protecting undeveloped land and creating affordable opportunities for homeownership. According to the Lowcountry Land Trust, the 102-acre Humbert Woods property will become a 97-acre nature preserve, while another five acres will be designated for affordable homes beside Sea Island Habitat for Humanity’s Sweetgrass Preserve neighbourhood. The housing effort is planned as a 50-home community for local families earning up to 80% of the area median income. The wider Charleston County conservation programme is also protecting hundreds of additional acres beyond Humbert Woods.A former development site will become protected landHumbert Woods is one of the largest remaining undeveloped parcels on northern Johns Island. Before the conservation project, the 102-acre property was zoned for more than 30 homes, meaning residential development was already a possible future for the land. Instead, the Lowcountry Land Trust identified the property as a conservation priority because of its forests, freshwater wetlands and connection to other protected areas on Johns Island. More than 97 acres contain upland forests and freshwater wetlands, according to the organisation. Keeping most of the property undeveloped is expected to provide several environmental benefits. The land can support wildlife habitat, help improve water quality and store floodwaters, while also retaining part of the rural landscape that has traditionally characterised Johns Island.The plan also means the protected land will not simply be closed off from the community. Lowcountry Land Trust and Sea Island Habitat for Humanity are working on plans for trails that will provide public access to the future Humbert Woods nature preserve. Charleston County's Greenbelt funding documents also describe walking trails, a small parking area and designated picnic space as part of the preservation plan.Five acres will make room for affordable homesThe other side of the project focuses on housing. Five acres of the Humbert Woods property have been designated for affordable homes next to the Sea Island Habitat for Humanity's Sweetgrass Preserve neighbourhood. Sea Island Habitat describes Sweetgrass Preserve as a planned 50-home community consisting of one, two and three-bedroom homes for local families earning up to 80% of the area median income. The organisation says the homes are intended for working local families, including people employed in sectors such as hospitality, retail and service industries. The broader goal is to make it possible for people who work in the area to also afford to live there. Habitat's model is different from simply giving homes away. Its homeownership programme provides partner families with affordable housing through zero-interest Habitat mortgages.According to the Sea Island Habitat's programme, Habitat homes are not free and that affordability comes through no-profit, interest-free loans and volunteer contributions. Sea Island Habitat's latest annual report says it surpassed its $4 million capital campaign target to fund Sweetgrass Preserve, the planned 50-home affordable neighbourhood.Conservation and housing planned side by sideWhat makes the Humbert Woods project notable is the way the two goals are being planned together. Instead of treating conservation and affordable housing as competing uses of land, the partnership divides the property between them. Most of Humbert Woods will remain protected, while a smaller portion will support affordable housing alongside the planned Sweetgrass Preserve development.Lowcountry Land Trust says the newly acquired property will expand the setting around the housing community and give residents access to nature close to their homes. The organisations are also working together on the future trail network. For Johns Island, that balance is particularly relevant as development continues to change the area. Only about 8% of Johns Island is permanently protected, while Humbert Woods is part of a network of other properties expected to become publicly accessible, including Grayson Oaks, Main Road Park, Simmons Creek and the Angel Oak Preserve.The land also carries a piece of Johns Island historyThe property has a cultural connection to the island as well as an environmental one. Lowcountry Land Trust points to maps dating to 1927 that identify the nearby Humbert Wood Public Elementary School. The school was associated with Mamie Elizabeth Garvin Fields, described by the organisation as one of the first African American public school teachers hired in Charleston County. She taught there early in her career. Preserving the surrounding landscape therefore also helps retain part of the area's historical identity as Johns Island develops. The project is not only about creating a new nature preserve; it is also about keeping a piece of the island's landscape and heritage intact.Public funding is helping protect the propertyThe Humbert Woods project is being supported by several funding sources, including Lowcountry Land Trust's Opportunity Fund, the Charleston County Greenbelt Program, the South Carolina Conservation Bank and the Charleston County Affordable Housing Land Acquisition Fund. Charleston County separately approved $3.63 million in Greenbelt funding for the Humbert Woods project, with $1.2805 million in applicant matching funds. County documents identify 97.1 acres for protection and a 5.8-acre portion for a separate affordable housing project. The preserved portion is planned to include public walking trails, parking and picnic space.The county's conservation effort is much larger than Humbert Woods. In a 2026 funding round, Charleston County approved more than $11.5 million for five projects expected to protect more than 900 acres countywide. That figure includes properties beyond Johns Island and should not be attributed entirely to the Humbert Woods project.A different way to think about growthThe Humbert Woods partnership is still developing. Sea Island Habitat for Humanity says it is in the early stages of land planning for the homes, while the housing organisation and Lowcountry Land Trust are working together on plans for trails through the future preserve. Still, the basic division of the land is clear: roughly 97 acres are intended to remain protected, while a much smaller portion will contribute to an affordable-homeownership effort. For a rapidly changing Johns Island, the project offers a way to approach growth without treating new housing and open space as entirely separate priorities. The result is planned to be a neighbourhood where families can build homes while a large stretch of the surrounding landscape remains available for wildlife, conservation and public recreation.You use AI every day.
